traces.summary:
CO2 methanation (Sabatier: CO2 + 4H2 ⇌ CH4 + 2H2O, ΔH°298 ≈ −165 kJ/mol) is strongly exothermic and therefore equilibrium-limited at high temperature, while it is kinetically limited at low temperature. The universal consequence for a temperature-programmed (light-off) experiment is a characteristic "volcano" in CH4 yield: the CO2-conversion / CH4-concentration trace rises sigmoidally out of a kinetic dead zone (typically 150–250 °C onset), reaches near-equilibrium (often 80–99% conversion for good Ni/Ru catalysts) somewhere in 300–400 °C, then FOLLOWS the declining thermodynamic equilibrium ceiling downward above ~400 °C. Where the observed curve peaks depends on catalyst activity: Ru catalysts light off lowest (T50 often 180–250 °C, near-100% CH4 selectivity), Ni is the workhorse (T50 ≈ 300–350 °C, max conversion ~80–95% at 350–400 °C, CH4 selectivity >95–99% below 400 °C), Co is similar-to-slightly-higher, and Fe is more active for the competing RWGS and thus makes more CO. On zeolite supports the same physics holds with support-specific activity: e.g. 6% Ni/zeolite-Y gives ~60% CO2 conversion at 300 °C / 1 MPa / 99% CH4 selectivity; Ni/NaY reaches ~21% at 200 °C with 100% CH4 selectivity; Ni on 5A/13X reaches 70–71% conversion with 92–96% CH4 selectivity; higher Si/Al (more hydrophobic, e.g. ZSM-5, BEA, silicalite) tends to raise low-temperature activity.

The CO byproduct is governed by the reverse water-gas shift (RWGS: CO2 + H2 ⇌ CO + H2O, ΔH° = +41 kJ/mol), which is endothermic and therefore increasingly favored as temperature rises. CO is essentially undetectable below ~350–400 °C (CH4 selectivity ≈ 100%) and grows monotonically above it, so CH4 selectivity is a decreasing sigmoid in temperature and CO selectivity a mirror-image increasing sigmoid. This is why the CO trace is near-zero at low T and rises at high T, and why the CH4 concentration trace bends over and declines: both equilibrium conversion falling AND selectivity shifting toward CO reduce CH4 above ~400 °C. Thermodynamic equilibrium CO2 conversion at 1 bar with stoichiometric H2/CO2 = 4 is ~0.99 below 300 °C, ~0.97 at 350 °C, ~0.85–0.90 at 400 °C, ~0.75–0.80 at 450 °C, and ~0.6–0.65 at 500 °C (pressure raises all of these because methanation reduces total moles).

For generating realistic synthetic demo curves, the cleanest and physically faithful construction is a product of two factors: a composition-dependent kinetic light-off sigmoid L(T) and a (nearly) composition-independent thermodynamic equilibrium ceiling X_eq(T), so X_obs(T) = X_eq(T)·L(T). Selectivity is a separate decreasing sigmoid S_CH4(T) whose midpoint T_sel and depth σ encode how much a given composition promotes RWGS/CO. The three outlet traces are then c_CH4 ∝ X_obs·S_CH4 (volcano), c_CO ∝ X_obs·(1−S_CH4) (rises at high T), c_CO2 ∝ (1−X_obs) (falls then recovers as equilibrium relaxes). The baseline figure of merit ∫ c_CH4 dT is a smooth scalar functional of the light-off temperature, width, equilibrium ceiling and selectivity, so it is well-suited to GP regression and Bayesian optimization over the metal-fraction simplex.

The rigorous alternative to the phenomenological ceiling is to compute X_eq(T,P,feed) exactly by simultaneously solving the two equilibrium relations for the methanation and RWGS extents; standard temperature-explicit equilibrium-constant correlations exist (Koschany 2016 for methanation; Moe/Gao WGS correlation for RWGS). Reaction rates for fitting real curves are best taken from the Koschany et al. (2016) Langmuir-Hinshelwood-Hougen-Watson expression, the community-standard intrinsic kinetic model for CO2 methanation on Ni, which already contains the reversibility term that makes the rate go to zero at equilibrium and thereby reproduces the high-temperature decline automatically.
key_equations_or_algorithms: REACTIONS AND ENTHALPIES (standard, 298 K). (R1) CO2 methanation / Sabatier: CO2 + 4 H2 <=> CH4 + 2 H2O, dH0 = -165 kJ/mol, mole change dn = -2 (equilibrium-limited, exothermic). (R2) Reverse water-gas shift (RWGS): CO2 + H2 <=> CO + H2O, dH0 = +41.1 kJ/mol, dn = 0 (endothermic; source of CO byproduct at high T). (R3) CO methanation: CO + 3 H2 <=> CH4 + H2O, dH0 = -206.3 kJ/mol. Note R1 = R2 + R3. These three fix the whole qualitative picture: R1 wins at low T, R2 (CO make) grows at high T.

EQUILIBRIUM CONSTANTS vs TEMPERATURE (T in Kelvin, R = 8.314 J/mol/K). Methanation (Koschany et al. 2016 correlation): Keq_meth(T) = 137 * T^(-3.998) * exp(158700 / (R*T)), units bar^-2. Sanity checks: ~1.3e6 bar^-2 at 555 K, ~1.5e2 bar^-2 at 723 K (falls fast with T -> equilibrium conversion declines). RWGS (from Moe WGS correlation, dimensionless since dn=0): K_WGS(T) = exp(4577.8/T - 4.33) for CO+H2O->CO2+H2, so K_RWGS(T) = 1/K_WGS(T) = exp(4.33 - 4577.8/T). K_RWGS ~1.6e-5 at 298 K but ~0.13 at 723 K, i.e. CO formation is negligible at low T and rises with T. General route if you prefer NASA/Shomate polynomials: Keq_j(T) = exp(-dG_j0(T)/(R*T)) with dG_j0(T) = dH_j0(T) - T*dS_j0(T).

EXACT EQUILIBRIUM CONVERSION (rigorous X_eq for the demo ceiling). Unknowns: extents xi1 (methanation), xi2 (RWGS). Feed basis n_CO2_0, n_H2_0 (stoich H2/CO2=4 => n_H2_0=4*n_CO2_0), optional inert n_in. Species moles: n_CO2 = n_CO2_0 - xi1 - xi2; n_H2 = n_H2_0 - 4*xi1 - xi2; n_CH4 = xi1; n_CO = xi2; n_H2O = 2*xi1 + xi2; n_tot = n_CO2_0 + n_H2_0 + n_in - 2*xi1. Partial pressures p_i = (n_i/n_tot)*P. Solve the 2 coupled equations: Keq_meth = (p_CH4 * p_H2O^2) / (p_CO2 * p_H2^4) and K_RWGS = (p_CO * p_H2O) / (p_CO2 * p_H2). Then X_eq = (xi1+xi2)/n_CO2_0 and equilibrium CH4 selectivity S_eq = xi1/(xi1+xi2). Solve with scipy.optimize.fsqp/least_squares over a T grid; representative results at 1 bar, H2/CO2=4: X_eq ~0.99 (<=300 C), ~0.97 (350 C), ~0.87 (400 C), ~0.78 (450 C), ~0.63 (500 C); CO fraction of converted CO2 climbs from ~0 below 350 C to a few percent by 450-500 C. Raising P shifts all X_eq up (Le Chatelier, dn<0).

PHENOMENOLOGICAL EQUILIBRIUM CEILING (fast closed form for synthetic data, replaces the solve if you don't want a nonlinear solver). Decreasing logistic in temperature: X_eq(T) = X_hi - (X_hi - X_lo) / (1 + exp( -(T - T_eq)/w_eq )). Suggested 1-atm parameters: X_hi = 0.99 (low-T plateau), X_lo = 0.45 (high-T floor at 550 C), T_eq = 490 C (midpoint of decline), w_eq = 55 C. For elevated pressure raise X_lo and T_eq. T in deg C throughout.

KOSCHANY et al. (2016) LHHW INTRINSIC RATE (community-standard model to FIT real curves; reversibility term auto-produces the high-T decline). r_CH4 = [ k * p_H2^0.5 * p_CO2^0.5 * (1 - beta) ] / [ 1 + K_OH*(p_H2O / p_H2^0.5) + K_H2*p_H2^0.5 + K_mix*p_CO2^0.5 ]^2, where the approach-to-equilibrium factor beta = (p_CH4 * p_H2O^2) / (p_CO2 * p_H2^4 * Keq_meth(T)) goes to 1 at equilibrium so r_CH4 -> 0. Best-fit parameters referenced to Tref = 555 K: k(Tref) = 3.46e-4 mol/(bar*s*g_cat), EA = 77.5 kJ/mol; K_OH(Tref) = 0.5 bar^-0.5, dH_OH = 22.4 kJ/mol; K_H2(Tref) = 0.44 bar^-0.5, dH_H2 = -6.2 kJ/mol; K_mix(Tref) = 0.88 bar^-0.5, dH_mix = -10 kJ/mol. Temperature dependence: k(T) = k(Tref)*exp[ -(EA/R)*(1/T - 1/Tref) ]; K_i(T) = K_i(Tref)*exp[ -(dH_i/R)*(1/T - 1/Tref) ]. (Verify exact coefficients against the primary paper; they are the standard values quoted across the literature.)

SYNTHETIC-CURVE GENERATIVE MODEL (recommended for demo data; composition x on the simplex, sum(x_i)=1). Step 1 map composition to descriptors: light-off temperature T50(x) = sum_i x_i*T50_i - sum_{i<j} b_ij*x_i*x_j + noise (bilinear terms encode bimetallic synergy); light-off width w(x) ~ 20-40 C; selectivity-rolloff midpoint T_sel(x) (temperature where CO appears); max CO fraction sigma(x) in [0,1]. Suggested per-metal anchors (deg C): T50_Ru~210, T50_Ni~320, T50_Co~340, T50_Fe~380; sigma_Ru~0.02, sigma_Ni~0.06, sigma_Co~0.10, sigma_Fe~0.35; T_sel_Fe lower (~380) than Ni/Ru (~440). Step 2 kinetic light-off L(T) = 1/(1+exp( -(T - T50)/w )). Step 3 observed conversion X_obs(T) = X_eq(T) * L(T). Step 4 CH4 selectivity S_CH4(T) = 1 - sigma/(1+exp( -(T - T_sel)/w_sel )), w_sel ~ 30 C. Step 5 normalized outlet signals (per inlet CO2): c_CH4(T) = X_obs(T)*S_CH4(T); c_CO(T) = X_obs(T)*(1 - S_CH4(T)); c_CO2(T) = 1 - X_obs(T). (Optional true mole fractions: with 1 mol CO2 + 4 mol H2 feed, CH4=X_obs*S_CH4, CO=X_obs*(1-S_CH4), H2O=2*CH4+CO, H2_out=4-4*CH4-CO, n_tot=5-2*CH4; y_i=n_i/n_tot.) Step 6 noise: add Gaussian ~1-3% absolute per channel plus small T jitter and baseline drift. This yields the correct volcano CH4 trace, monotone-rising CO trace, and falling-then-recovering CO2 trace over T in [150,500] C.

FIGURES OF MERIT. Baseline: FOM = integral over T of c_CH4(T) dT (trapezoidal, np.trapz), a smooth scalar increasing with catalyst activity (lower T50), higher equilibrium ceiling, and higher selectivity. Complementary FOMs worth exposing as separate GP targets: T50 (light-off temperature, minimize), peak CH4 yield max_T c_CH4(T) and its argmax T_peak, maximum CO2 conversion max_T X_obs, integral CO make integral c_CO dT (minimize / constraint), and operating-window width = measure{ T : c_CH4(T) > tau } for threshold tau. Normalize each FOM by its theoretical equilibrium maximum integral(X_eq dT) so targets are comparable across supports/pressures.
design_recommendations: Represent every measured trace by a small parametric curve model, not raw points: fit (T50, w, T_sel, w_sel, sigma) per curve against the product form X_eq(T)*L(T) with the universal X_eq(T) held fixed (computed once per P, feed). This 5-parameter latent captures light-off, ceiling and CO rolloff and gives a low-dimensional, physically interpretable target vector for the downstream GPs; it also regularizes noisy tails.

Keep the thermodynamic equilibrium ceiling X_eq(T,P,feed) as a fixed, catalyst-independent module (either the exact 2-extent solve or the logistic closed form). Only the kinetic/selectivity parameters are catalyst-dependent. This separation makes the models physically honest (no catalyst can beat equilibrium) and drastically shrinks what the GP must learn.

Use the Koschany LHHW rate law (with its built-in reversibility factor beta) as the mechanistic option for fitting real light-off curves in a plug-flow reactor model; integrate dX/dW = r_CH4/F_CO2_0 down the bed. Because r_CH4 -> 0 as beta -> 1, this reproduces the high-temperature equilibrium decline without any ad hoc capping. Expose the Arrhenius pre-factor/EA (and effective active-site density) as the composition-dependent parameters the GP predicts.

Baseline FOM = np.trapz(c_CH4, T). Also compute and store T50, peak CH4 yield, max conversion, and integral-CO as auxiliary/constraint objectives; batch BO can then do multi-objective (maximize CH4 integral while constraining CO make) which matches the real catalytic goal better than CH4 alone.

For the chained GP with uncertainty propagation: GP_A maps selected composition -> actual (measured) composition (learns the synthesis realization error / simplex distortion); GP_B maps actual composition -> curve-parameter vector or FOM. Propagate by Monte-Carlo: sample actual composition from GP_A posterior, push each sample through GP_B, aggregate to get a predictive mean+variance at the SELECTED composition (law of total variance). Alternatively linearize (moment matching) for speed. Model curve-parameter GPs with independent or multi-output (LMC/ICM) kernels; a Matern-5/2 kernel on the composition simplex is a good default.

Handle the simplex constraint (sum of metal fractions = 1) explicitly in both the GP and the acquisition optimizer. Options: (a) isometric-log-ratio (ILR) or additive-log-ratio transform to an unconstrained R^(k-1) space for the GP; (b) optimize the batch acquisition directly on the simplex with a projected/soft-max parameterization. Avoid modeling in raw redundant coordinates.

For batch Bayesian optimization of ~6 points per round, use a joint batch acquisition: qEI / qNEI / qUCB or q-Thompson sampling (BoTorch), or greedy sequential with local penalization / fantasy (Kriging Believer) to enforce batch diversity. Include the GP_A realization noise as heteroscedastic input noise so the optimizer does not over-trust compositions that are hard to synthesize accurately.

Make temperature grid and pressure first-class metadata: X_eq and thus every FOM depend on P and H2/CO2 ratio. Store them with each curve and recompute the equilibrium ceiling per condition so FOMs are comparable and the GP is not confounded by operating-condition drift.

For the synthetic demo generator, seed per-metal anchors (T50, sigma, T_sel) and bilinear bimetallic-synergy terms b_ij, then add correlated noise. This produces realistic volcano CH4 traces, monotone-rising CO traces, and non-trivial optima on the simplex (synergistic bimetallics beating pure metals) so the active-learning loop has something real to discover.

Validate the generator against literature anchors before trusting it: Ni light-off ~300-350 C with 80-95% max conversion and >95% CH4 selectivity below 400 C; Ru light-off <=250 C near-100% selectivity; CO essentially zero below ~350 C then rising; CH4 yield peak near 350-400 C for Ni. If your synthetic curves violate these, adjust anchors, not the physics.

caveats: Exact Koschany kinetic parameter values (k=3.46e-4, EA=77.5 kJ/mol, K_OH=0.5/dH=22.4, K_H2=0.44/dH=-6.2, K_mix=0.88/dH=-10, Tref=555 K) are quoted from memory of the standard literature values because publisher pages (ScienceDirect, KIT) returned site-level 403 to the fetch tool; re-verify against the primary paper before hard-coding, especially units (bar vs kPa) and Tref.

The methanation equilibrium-constant form Keq=137*T^-3.998*exp(158700/RT) [bar^-2] and the RWGS form K_RWGS=exp(4.33-4577.8/T) are widely used correlations; for publication-grade equilibrium curves compute Keq from NASA/Shomate thermochemistry (dG0(T)) instead, which is exact and consistent across all three reactions.

Numeric equilibrium CO2 conversions I give (0.99 at <300 C down to ~0.63 at 500 C, 1 bar, H2/CO2=4) are representative literature values; the precise numbers depend on pressure, H2/CO2 ratio and inert dilution and should be recomputed for your exact conditions with the 2-extent solve.

All numeric content here therefore comes from search-result abstracts plus established thermochemistry, not full-text extraction; validate key numbers against full texts.

The phenomenological logistic X_eq(T) and the synthetic per-metal anchor values (T50, sigma, T_sel, synergy terms) are engineering conveniences for generating demo data, not measured constants; tune them so generated curves match the literature anchors listed in the design recommendations.

Continuous multimetallic (simplex) composition screening for CO2 methanation is thin in the literature; most reported multimetallic work is discrete bimetallic ratios (Ni-Fe, Ni-Co, Ni-Ru, Ru/NiO-CeO2). Expect to rely on the generative model and your own active-learning campaign rather than a dense literature prior over the simplex.

SSZ-13 (CHA) and pure-silica silicalite are less represented than ZSM-5, BEA, FAU (Y), 5A and 13X for methanation supports; if those specific frameworks are central, budget dedicated experiments since prior data is sparse.

fom.summary:
Figures of merit (FOMs) for ranking catalysts from temperature-vs-concentration (light-off / temperature-programmed reaction) traces fall into four families. (1) Point metrics on the conversion/yield-vs-T curve: light-off temperatures T10/T50/T90 (temperature at which conversion or yield first crosses 10/50/90 %; lower is better; T50 is the field-standard descriptor), onset temperature, and conversion/yield/selectivity evaluated at a fixed reference temperature. (2) Rate/productivity metrics: space-time yield (STY, mol or g CH4 per g or per cm3 catalyst per hour) and turnover frequency (TOF, molecules converted per active site per second). (3) Integral / area-under-curve metrics over a temperature window — the requested baseline ∫C_CH4 dT is one instance; the automotive light-off community uses the direct analog (cumulative tailpipe emissions = time/temperature integral of (1−conversion)), and high-throughput serial temperature-programmed screening rigs reduce each ramp to scalar scores. (4) Multi-objective treatments that keep activity, selectivity and stability separate and combine them by scalarization (weighted sum, augmented Chebyshev, Derringer–Suich desirability) or by Pareto/hypervolume methods.

For CO2 methanation specifically, two domain facts should shape FOM design. First, the Sabatier reaction CO2 + 4H2 → CH4 + 2H2O is strongly exothermic (ΔH ≈ −165 kJ/mol), so the equilibrium CO2 conversion FALLS with rising temperature; real conversion-vs-T curves rise under kinetic control, reach a maximum, then plateau or decline as they hit the equilibrium ceiling (best Ru/Ce catalysts already sit near the thermodynamic limit). Second, the parallel endothermic reverse water-gas-shift (CO2 + H2 → CO + H2O) makes CO the main by-product, so CH4 selectivity degrades at high T. Both facts mean a raw ∫C_CH4 dT over a wide window rewards high-temperature area that is largely a thermodynamic property shared by all catalysts and can be dominated by CO-contaminated high-T operation. The robust fixes are to (a) integrate the dimensionless CH4 yield Y_CH4 = X_CO2·S_CH4 rather than raw outlet concentration (feed/dilution-invariant and selectivity-aware), (b) normalize by window width to get a mean yield, and (c) optionally normalize by the temperature-resolved equilibrium yield to isolate catalyst merit from thermodynamics.

The central critique of any single integral is that it collapses curve shape: two catalysts with identical area can differ drastically — one lighting off early and narrow, the other broad and high-T — yet only the early-light-off catalyst is operationally valuable (lower heating cost, less sintering). The SAE 3-way-catalyst literature documents exactly this, showing light-off curve shape, not just T50, drives cumulative emissions. Therefore the integral should never be the sole FOM. It should be reported alongside the T10/T50/T90 triple (which encodes onset, midpoint and steepness/shape), the maximum yield and its temperature, and a low-temperature-weighted integral that explicitly rewards activity at low T via a monotone-decreasing weight w(T) (e.g. 1/T, an exponential decay, or an energy/exergy-cost weight). Selectivity and stability should be tracked as their own FOMs, not folded silently into an activity integral.

For the package's batch Bayesian optimization (6 points/round over the metal-fraction simplex), keep the FOMs as a vector objective and prefer native multi-objective batch acquisition (hypervolume-based qNEHVI/qEHVI) that returns a Pareto set of activity/selectivity/low-T trade-offs; expose scalarizers (weighted sum, augmented Chebyshev, Derringer–Suich desirability) only as a single-objective fallback or when a firm priority exists, and support constrained formulations (maximize activity subject to S_CH4 ≥ threshold) since selectivity is often a hard requirement. Crucially, because the curves come from chained GPs with uncertainty, exploit that every integral FOM is a linear functional of the predicted curve, so its posterior is Gaussian in closed form (mean = quadrature-weighted posterior mean, variance = quadrature-weighted posterior covariance); nonlinear FOMs (T50, yield ratios, approach-to-equilibrium) get Monte-Carlo propagation over posterior curve samples.
key_equations_or_algorithms: CO2 conversion (carbon balance): X_CO2(T) = (n_CH4,out + n_CO,out) / (n_CO2,out + n_CH4,out + n_CO,out), equivalently X_CO2 = (F_CO2,in - F_CO2,out)/F_CO2,in. n_i = molar flow of species i at reactor outlet; F_CO2,in = CO2 molar feed rate. Dimensionless in [0,1]. Use the carbon-balance form when only outlet concentrations are measured.

CH4 selectivity (carbon basis): S_CH4(T) = n_CH4,out / (n_CH4,out + n_CO,out). If other carbon products are present, add them to the denominator. Dimensionless in [0,1]; separates 'makes CH4' from 'makes CO' (the RWGS by-product).

CH4 yield: Y_CH4(T) = X_CO2(T) * S_CH4(T) = n_CH4,out / n_CO2,in. Dimensionless in [0,1]. RECOMMENDED base quantity for every FOM (feed-, flow- and dilution-invariant and selectivity-aware), in place of raw outlet CH4 concentration C_CH4.

Light-off temperatures: T_p = smallest T such that Y_CH4(T) = p (or X_CO2(T)=p) on the rising branch, for p in {0.10, 0.50, 0.90}; T_onset at p ~= 0.05. Obtain by monotone interpolation (PCHIP) of the rising branch and take the FIRST up-crossing to be robust to high-T equilibrium roll-off. Lower T_p is better. Reporting the triple (T10,T50,T90) encodes onset, midpoint and steepness/shape that a single number loses.

Baseline integral FOM as requested: I_CH4 = INT_{T_lo}^{T_hi} C_CH4(T) dT (trapezoidal). C_CH4 = outlet CH4 concentration; [T_lo,T_hi] = integration window. NOTE units are concentration*K and value depends on feed/dilution. Recommended replacements: yield-area A_Y = INT_{T_lo}^{T_hi} Y_CH4(T) dT (units K), and window-normalized MEAN YIELD Ybar = A_Y/(T_hi - T_lo) (dimensionless, in [0,1], comparable across windows).

Low-temperature-weighted (operating-cost) yield score: S_w = [ INT w(T) Y_CH4(T) dT ] / [ INT w(T) dT ], with monotone-decreasing weight w(T). Options: w(T)=1/T; w(T)=exp(-(T - T_lo)/tau) (tau sets how sharply low-T is favored); or energy-cost weight w(T) ∝ 1/Q(T) with Q(T)=sensible heat to reach T. Rewards CH4 produced at low temperature; reduces to Ybar when w is constant.

Approach-to-equilibrium efficiency: eta(T) = Y_CH4(T) / Y_eq(T), where Y_eq(T) is the equilibrium CH4 yield from Gibbs-free-energy minimization of {CO2+4H2<=>CH4+2H2O, CO2+H2<=>CO+H2O} at (T, P, H2/CO2 ratio). Integral form A_eta = INT eta(T) dT / (T_hi - T_lo). Equilibrium constant via van't Hoff: ln K(T) = -DeltaG_rxn(T)/(R T); with DeltaH_methanation ~= -165 kJ/mol, K decreases with T (conversion ceiling falls). eta removes the shared thermodynamic ceiling so the FOM reflects catalyst quality, not equilibrium.

Productivity metrics: Space-time yield STY_CH4 = (Y_CH4 * F_CO2,in * M_CH4)/m_cat  [g_CH4 g_cat^-1 h^-1] (or per catalyst volume). Turnover frequency TOF = (X_CO2 * F_CO2,in)/N_sites  [s^-1], with N_sites = (w_metal * D)/M_metal, D = metal dispersion, w_metal = active-metal mass, M_metal = molar mass. Requires site count / mass, which may not be derivable from the T-vs-C curve alone.

Scalarization of a normalized FOM vector f~ (activity, low-T score, selectivity, stability), each mapped to [0,1]: (a) Weighted sum J = SUM_i w_i f~_i (simple; cannot reach non-convex Pareto regions). (b) Augmented Chebyshev J = max_i w_i |f~_i - z*_i| + rho * SUM_i |f~_i - z*_i| (z* = ideal point, rho small; reaches non-convex fronts; basis of random-scalarization MOBO). (c) Derringer-Suich desirability: one-sided-max d_i = ((f_i - L_i)/(U_i - L_i))^r for L_i<=f_i<=U_i (0 below L_i, 1 above U_i); overall D = (PROD_i d_i^{w_i})^{1/SUM_i w_i}; D=0 if any d_i=0 gives hard-constraint semantics (e.g. selectivity floor).

Uncertainty propagation for chained-GP curves: any linear-functional FOM L[f] = INT a(T) f(T) dT with f ~ GP(mu, k) is Gaussian in closed form: mean = a_vec^T mu_vec, var = a_vec^T K a_vec, where a_vec are quadrature weights (trapezoid/Simpson or w(T)-weighted), mu_vec = posterior mean at nodes, K_{jk} = k(T_j,T_k) posterior covariance. Applies to I_CH4, A_Y, Ybar, S_w. For NONLINEAR FOMs (T50, Y_max, eta, ratios) draw posterior curve samples and compute the FOM on each sample (Monte Carlo) to get its predictive mean/variance for the BO acquisition.
design_recommendations: Compute derived dimensionless curves X_CO2(T), S_CH4(T), Y_CH4(T) as a first pass, and build EVERY FOM on yield/conversion, not on raw outlet concentration, so scores are invariant to feed dilution and total flow. Still implement the requested raw INT C_CH4 dT for backward compatibility, but flag it as feed-dependent and default users to the yield-area A_Y / mean-yield Ybar.

Ship a FOM registry with a uniform interface fom(curve) -> (value, variance). Built-ins to include: mean-yield Ybar / yield-area A_Y; T10/T50/T90 and T_onset; Y_max and T_at_Ymax; yield@T_ref and conversion@T_ref; low-T-weighted score S_w (pluggable weight w(T)); CH4 selectivity (mean and @T_ref) and CO co-production; approach-to-equilibrium eta and its integral A_eta; STY and TOF (when site/mass data are supplied).

Make the integration window [T_lo,T_hi] an explicit, required, logged parameter; normalize integrals by window width so FOMs are mean-yield-like and comparable across rounds/windows. Define and log an extrapolation policy (clip vs GP-extrapolate vs NaN) when a measured or predicted curve does not span the window, and warn on partial coverage — integral scores are otherwise not comparable.

Use PCHIP / monotone interpolation for light-off temperature extraction, take the first up-crossing (robust to the equilibrium roll-off/decline at high T that CO2 methanation curves exhibit), and return NaN with a reason code when a threshold is never reached rather than silently extrapolating.

Include a thermodynamic-equilibrium submodule that returns Y_eq(T), X_eq(T) and S_eq(T) as functions of (T, P, H2/CO2 ratio, inerts), via equilibrium constants from DeltaG(T) (NASA polynomials / van't Hoff) or a Gibbs minimizer (e.g. Cantera). This powers the approach-to-equilibrium FOM eta and lets the package warn when a data point is operating in the equilibrium-limited regime where activity ranking is meaningless.

Exploit the linear-functional structure for uncertainty: implement analytic Gaussian propagation (value = a^T mu, var = a^T K a) for all integral FOMs directly from the chained-GP posterior mean and covariance at the quadrature nodes, and Monte-Carlo posterior-sample propagation for nonlinear FOMs (T50, Y_max, eta, ratios). Return (mean, variance) or raw samples so the batch-BO acquisition (qNEHVI/EI) can consume calibrated uncertainty.

Keep FOMs as a VECTOR objective and prefer native multi-objective batch Bayesian optimization with a hypervolume acquisition (qNEHVI or qEHVI, e.g. BoTorch) for the 6-point batches; it returns a Pareto set of activity/low-T/selectivity trade-offs. Offer scalarizers (weighted sum, augmented Chebyshev, Derringer-Suich desirability) as a single-objective fallback or when the user asserts a firm priority; random-scalarization batches are a lightweight alternative to hypervolume.

Support a constrained formulation (maximize an activity FOM subject to S_CH4 >= s_min, or subject to a stability/deactivation bound) via constrained EI, because selectivity and stability are frequently hard requirements rather than smooth trade-offs; Derringer-Suich desirability with a lower spec limit gives the same hard-floor semantics inside a scalarized pipeline.

Never expose the single integral as the lone ranking score in the UI/report. Always co-report the T10/T50/T90 triple, Y_max and its temperature, and the low-T-weighted score, because an integral cannot distinguish early-narrow light-off from broad-high-T activity (documented in automotive light-off literature) — the very discrimination this catalyst program cares about.

Record FOM provenance (window bounds, weight function and its parameters, interpolation method, equilibrium P and H2/CO2 ratio) with each computed score so rankings are reproducible and comparable across active-learning rounds as the dataset grows.

references.citation: Molinet-Chinaglia, C. et al. 'Low Temperature Sabatier CO2 Methanation.' ChemCatChem, 2024, e202401213.
references.relevance: Review of low-temperature CO2 methanation; motivates low-T-weighted FOMs and documents the exothermic equilibrium ceiling and RWGS/CO selectivity trade-off that a raw high-T integral misrepresents.

references.citation: SAE Technical Paper 2021-01-0594. 'A Study of the Effect of Light-Off Temperatures and Light-Off Curve Shape on the Cumulative Emissions Performance of 3-Way Catalytic Converters.' 2021.
references.relevance: Primary automotive precedent that cumulative (integral) performance depends on light-off CURVE SHAPE, not T50 alone; underpins the critique that a single scalar integral loses shape information and the recommendation to co-report T10/T50/T90 (paywalled; abstract used).

references.citation: Nature Catalysis 6, 2023. 'Light-driven CO2 methanation over Au-grafted Ce0.95Ru0.05O2 solid-solution catalysts with activities approaching the thermodynamic limit.'
references.relevance: Demonstrates state-of-the-art catalysts operate near the equilibrium ceiling, justifying an approach-to-equilibrium FOM eta(T)=Y/Y_eq that removes the shared thermodynamic component from activity ranking.

references.citation: Kinetics, Model Discrimination, and Parameters Estimation of CO2 Methanation on Highly Active Ni/CeO2 Catalyst. Ind. Eng. Chem. Res., 2022, 61, acs.iecr.2c00164.
references.relevance: Primary source using T50 light-off (~303 C) and conversion/selectivity/yield definitions for a Ni/CeO2 methanation catalyst; template for the point FOMs and kinetic-model fitting the package must support.

references.citation: From CO2 to Methane: A Thermodynamic Study of the Sabatier Reaction for Clean Energy Applications. Proceedings 2025, 133, 001.
references.relevance: Provides equilibrium CO2 conversion vs temperature (exothermic, delta H ~= -165 kJ/mol; conversion falls above ~450 C), the data needed for the equilibrium submodule that computes Y_eq(T) and flags equilibrium-limited operating points.

references.citation: A generalized machine learning framework to predict the space-time yield of methanol from thermocatalytic CO2 hydrogenation. Appl. Catal. B, 2022 (S0926337322004714).
references.relevance: Defines space-time yield (STY) as a scalar productivity FOM and uses it as an ML regression target, directly paralleling the package's GP prediction of a scalar FOM from composition.

references.citation: Derringer, G.; Suich, R. 'Simultaneous Optimization of Several Response Variables.' Journal of Quality Technology, 1980, 12(4), 214-219.
references.relevance: Original desirability-function scalarization (one-sided/two-sided desirabilities combined by weighted geometric mean); the recommended scalarizer with hard-floor semantics for folding selectivity/stability constraints into a single objective.

references.citation: Paria, B.; Kandasamy, K.; Poczos, B. 'A Flexible Framework for Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization using Random Scalarizations.' arXiv:1805.12168 (UAI 2020).
references.relevance: Random (Chebyshev) scalarization approach to multi-objective Bayesian optimization; lightweight alternative to hypervolume for the batch BO over activity/selectivity/low-T objectives.

references.citation: Daulton, S.; Balandat, M.; Bakshy, E. 'Parallel Bayesian Optimization of Multiple Noisy Objectives with Expected Hypervolume Improvement (qNEHVI).' NeurIPS 2021, arXiv:2105.08195.
references.relevance: Batch, noise-robust hypervolume acquisition (BoTorch) — the recommended engine for the 6-point-per-round multi-objective batch BO returning a Pareto set of FOM trade-offs.

references.citation: Pareto optimization to accelerate multi-objective virtual screening. Digital Discovery, 2024, RSC, D3DD00227F.
references.relevance: Argues Pareto/hypervolume screening can outperform scalarization for competing objectives, supporting the recommendation to keep FOMs as a vector objective rather than always collapsing to one scalar.

references.citation: Adaptive Catalyst Discovery Using Multicriteria Bayesian Optimization with Representation Learning. arXiv:2404.12445 (2024).
references.relevance: Directly analogous multi-criteria Bayesian optimization for catalyst discovery, evidencing the vector-FOM + MOBO design pattern recommended for this package.

references.citation: Maximizing CH4 yield by thermodynamically optimizing the temperature profile of fixed-bed CO2 methanation reactors. (S2950487225000054), 2025.
references.relevance: Confirms that CH4 yield vs temperature is non-monotone with an equilibrium-limited high-T decline, justifying first-up-crossing light-off extraction and window-aware/equilibrium-normalized integral FOMs.

caveats: Several primary PDFs (SAE 2021-01-0594, some Wiley/RSC/PMC articles) returned HTTP 403 / paywall; the equations reported here are standard, textbook heterogeneous-catalysis definitions corroborated across multiple accessible sources rather than transcribed verbatim from a single locked paper.

Approach-to-equilibrium normalization (eta = Y/Y_eq) is only as good as the equilibrium model: Y_eq depends on P, H2/CO2 ratio, inerts and the reaction set included (methanation + RWGS at minimum); errors in Y_eq propagate directly into the FOM, and eta is ill-defined where Y_eq -> 0.

TOF and STY require active-site counts or catalyst mass/volume and dispersion that are generally NOT recoverable from the temperature-vs-concentration trace alone, so these FOMs may be uncomputable for some data points and should degrade gracefully.

The requested raw integral INT C_CH4 dT is feed-, flow- and dilution-dependent and selectivity-blind; it can rank a diluted high-yield catalyst below a concentrated low-yield one and can be inflated by equilibrium-limited high-T area, so it should not be used as the sole ranking FOM.

Light-off temperatures and other nonlinear FOMs have non-Gaussian predictive distributions under the chained-GP model; the closed-form linear-functional variance applies only to integral FOMs, and Monte-Carlo propagation (with enough samples) is needed for T50/Y_max/ratios to avoid miscalibrated BO uncertainty.

Scalarization choice materially changes the optimum: weighted-sum cannot reach non-convex Pareto regions, so a program that relies on it may systematically miss good trade-off catalysts that hypervolume/Chebyshev methods would find.

edbo.summary:
EDBO (Shields et al., Nature 2021) and EDBO+ (Garrido Torres et al., JACS 2022) are the Doyle lab's open-source Bayesian reaction-optimization packages. Both are built on GPyTorch (EDBO+ additionally on BoTorch) and both operate over a DISCRETE, fully enumerated candidate list (a pandas DataFrame / CSV "scope", one row per possible experiment) rather than a continuous domain — a key fact for our metal-fraction simplex: compositions must be discretized to a candidate grid before either package (or a faithful clone) can be used. EDBO (repo b-shields/edbo, PyPI 'edbo' 0.1.0, Nov 2020) exposes a `BO`/`BO_express` class: surrogate = exact GP with ConstantMean + ScaleKernel(Matern nu=2.5, ARD), Gaussian likelihood with noise floor 1e-5, targets standardized to zero mean/unit variance, MAP hyperparameter fitting by ADAM (lr 0.1, ~100 iters, optional restarts) on the exact marginal log-likelihood plus Gamma hyperpriors. Default acquisition is EI with batches built by the Kriging-believer algorithm (greedy EI -> insert posterior mean as pseudo-observation -> refit -> repeat q times); Thompson sampling (q joint posterior draws, argmax each), PI, UCB, MeanMax/VarMax, eps-greedy, and TS-hybrids are also implemented. EDBO+ (repo doyle-lab-ucla/edboplus, PyPI 'edboplus' 0.0.2, Nov 2022; installs a package still named 'edbo' v0.2.0) reworks this around BoTorch for multi-objective work: one independent SingleTaskGP per objective (same Matern-ARD kernel and nearly identical Gamma priors, ADAM 1000 iters lr 0.1), inputs MinMax-scaled to [0,1], each objective sign-flipped for 'min' then standardized by a custom EDBOStandardScaler; acquisition default is qNEHVI (q-Noisy Expected Hypervolume Improvement, alpha=0, incremental_nehvi=True, prune_baseline=True; falls back to MC qEI for a single objective) with a SobolQMCNormalSampler (512 MC samples, degraded to 256/128/64 for scopes >10k/50k/100k rows) and batch selection by BoTorch's optimize_acqf_discrete(choices=untested rows, q=batch, unique=True) which does sequential-greedy fantasy conditioning. The reference point for hypervolume is the per-objective minimum of the (scaled) observations unless user objective_thresholds are given. First-round initialization (no data yet) uses CVT sampling by default (via idaes-pse pysmo), with LHS and random as options.

The user-facing APIs differ substantially. EDBO: construct BO(domain=DataFrame_of_encoded_candidates, results=DataFrame_of_measured_rows, acquisition_function='EI', batch_size=5, init_method='rand', target='yield', plus kernel/prior kwargs), then bo.fit()/bo.run() -> bo.proposed_experiments; BO_express additionally auto-featurizes a reaction_components dict (encodings: 'ohe', 'numeric', 'smiles', 'resolve'/Mordred/DFT descriptor matrices) and auto-selects priors by dimensionality. EDBO+: EDBOplus().generate_reaction_scope(components={...}, filename='reaction.csv') builds the Cartesian-product scope CSV; each round you fill measured objective values into the CSV (unmeasured rows say 'PENDING') and call EDBOplus().run(objectives=['y1','y2'], objective_mode=['max','min'], batch=5, columns_features='all', init_sampling_method='cvt', seed=0, acquisition_function='NoisyEHVI'); it rewrites the CSV sorted by a new 'priority' column (1 = suggested next batch, -1 = already measured) and writes pred_<filename>.csv with per-candidate predicted_mean, predicted_std_dev and (raw-scale, per-objective, diagnostic-only) expected_improvement columns. Categorical columns are auto-one-hot-encoded with pandas get_dummies(drop_first=True); numeric columns (our continuous metal fractions) pass through and are MinMax-scaled, so continuous variables are supported ONLY as pre-enumerated candidate values.

Installability today (checked 2026-07): both are effectively frozen. edbo pins Python 3.7.5, gpytorch==1.0.0, pyro-ppl==1.1, pyclustering==0.9.3.1, pytorch 1.3.1 (conda instructions) — it does not install on any modern Python; treat it as reference code only. edboplus's setup.py pins botorch==0.5.0, gpytorch==1.5.1, torch==1.10.0, idaes-pse==1.5.1, numpy==1.21.5, pandas==1.3.4; torch 1.10 has wheels only through Python 3.9, and the code imports `botorch.sampling.samplers` (removed in botorch >=0.7/0.8) and `idaes.surrogate.pysmo` (moved in idaes 2.x), so it cannot run against current botorch/idaes — the working recipe is a dedicated conda env with Python 3.9 and `pip install -e .` from the git clone (the README's own instructions). Consequently the recommended architecture for our framework is: implement a BoTorch-native backend that REPLICATES EDBO+'s exact model choices (documented below with exact prior values read from source), plus a thin optional subprocess/CSV adapter to genuine edboplus in an isolated env, plus a GPy or scikit-learn fallback. GPy can match behavior closely (it supports Gamma priors and MAP); scikit-learn cannot encode hyperpriors (bounds + restarts only), so an sklearn fallback should be labeled behaviorally divergent.
key_equations_or_algorithms: EDBO/EDBO+ surrogate GP: f(x) ~ GP(m, k) with m(x) = c (gpytorch ConstantMean, learned scalar) and k(x,x') = sigma_f^2 * k_Matern52_ARD(x,x'), where k_Matern52_ARD = (1 + sqrt(5)*r + (5/3)*r^2) * exp(-sqrt(5)*r), r = sqrt( sum_{d=1..D} (x_d - x'_d)^2 / l_d^2 ). Variables: l_d = per-dimension (ARD) lengthscale, sigma_f^2 = outputscale (ScaleKernel), D = number of encoded features. Likelihood: y = f(x) + eps, eps ~ N(0, sigma_n^2), with hard constraint sigma_n^2 >= 1e-5 (GreaterThan noise constraint). Observations y are standardized before fitting: y_std = (y - mean(y_train)) / std(y_train). Matern nu is configurable in edbo (0.5/1.5/2.5) with default nu=2.5; edboplus uses gpytorch MaternKernel default, also nu=2.5.

Hyperpriors (gpytorch GammaPrior(alpha, beta) = shape/rate parameterization, density p(theta) proportional to theta^(alpha-1) * exp(-beta*theta), mean = alpha/beta; the prior log-density is ADDED to the marginal log-likelihood, i.e. MAP estimation). Exact values from source: (a) EDBO+ (edboplus model.py, hardcoded for every problem): lengthscale ~ Gamma(2.0, 0.2) with init l_d = 5.0; outputscale ~ Gamma(5.0, 0.5) with init sigma_f^2 = 8.0; noise ~ Gamma(1.5, 0.1) with init sigma_n^2 = 5.0; noise floor 1e-5. (b) edbo BO class defaults (bro.py): lengthscale ~ Gamma(2.0, 0.2) init 5.0; outputscale ~ Gamma(5.0, 0.5) init 8.0; noise ~ Gamma(1.5, 0.5) init 1.0. (c) edbo BO_express auto-selection by feature count: LOW-D (<5 features — the regime of our 3-4 component metal-fraction simplex): lengthscale ~ Gamma(1.2, 1.1) init 0.2, outputscale ~ Gamma(5.0, 0.5) init 8.0, noise ~ Gamma(1.05, 0.5) init 0.1; DFT-descriptor regime (<100 features): Gamma(2.0,0.2) init 5.0 / Gamma(5.0,0.5) init 8.0 / Gamma(1.5,0.1) init 5.0; Mordred high-D (>=100): Gamma(2.0,0.1) init 10.0 / Gamma(2.0,0.1) init 10.0 / Gamma(1.5,0.1) init 5.0; one-hot-encoded spaces: Gamma(3.0,1.0) init 2.0 / Gamma(5.0,0.2) init 20.0 / Gamma(1.5,0.1) init 5.0.

Hyperparameter fitting (both packages): theta_MAP = argmax_theta [ log p(y_std | X, theta) + sum_i log p_Gamma(theta_i) ] optimized with torch.optim.Adam on -ExactMarginalLogLikelihood; edbo: learning_rate=0.1, training_iters=100 (default), n_restarts=0 default (restarts jitter initial values); edboplus: lr=0.1, fixed 1000 iterations, no restarts, dtype=torch.double, CPU.

Expected improvement (edbo acq_func.py, computed on standardized y): z = (mu(x) - y_best - xi)/sigma(x); EI(x) = (mu(x) - y_best - xi) * Phi(z) + sigma(x) * phi(z), with jitter xi = 0.01, y_best = max observed standardized target, Phi/phi = standard normal CDF/PDF. (EDBO+ also writes a per-objective raw-scale EI diagnostic column using y_best = max/min of raw observations and xi = 0, with EI := 0 where sigma = 0 — but this column is reporting only; the acquisition actually optimized is qNEHVI/qEI.)

Batch selection, EDBO single-objective = Kriging believer (Ginsbourger-style constant-liar with lie = posterior mean): for j = 1..q: (1) evaluate EI over all remaining candidate rows; (2) pick argmax, excluding already-measured rows and rows already in the batch (duplicates=False default); (3) 'believe' y_hat_j = GP posterior mean at the chosen point and append (x_j, y_hat_j) to the training set; (4) re-instantiate and refit the GP (hyperparameters warm-started from previous MAP values) on the augmented data; repeat. Alternative batching: Thompson sampling — draw q independent joint samples f^(s) from the GP posterior over the full candidate matrix (chunked at 20000 rows for memory), select argmax of each sample with de-duplication; hybrids ('EI-TS' etc.) take 1 point by the named function and q-1 by TS. Full edbo acquisition menu: 'EI' (default), 'PI', 'UCB', 'TS', 'EI-TS', 'PI-TS', 'UCB-TS', 'rand-TS', 'MeanMax-TS', 'VarMax-TS', 'MeanMax', 'VarMax', 'rand', 'eps-greedy'.

EDBO+ multi-objective model: for M objectives, fit M independent SingleTaskGPs on the SAME MinMax-scaled X (scaler fit on training rows only: x' = (x - x_min)/(x_max - x_min)); objective preprocessing: if objective_mode[i]=='min' then y_i := -y_i; then per-objective standardization y_i' = (y_i - mu_i)/s_i with s_i floored at 1e-6 (EDBOStandardScaler); predictive variance is back-transformed as var_raw = var_std * s_i^2 and mean as mu_raw = mu_std * s_i + mu_i. Models are wrapped in botorch ModelListGP for the acquisition.

EDBO+ acquisition (default 'NoisyEHVI'): qNEHVI (Daulton et al. 2021), alpha_qNEHVI({x_1..x_q}) = E_f[ HV( P_n ∪ {f(x_1)..f(x_q)} ; r ) - HV( P_n ; r ) ] where HV(.;r) is the dominated hypervolume w.r.t. reference point r, P_n is the (posterior-sampled, noisy) set of already-observed points (X_baseline = scaled training X, prune_baseline=True, incremental_nehvi=True, alpha=0 i.e. exact box decomposition), and the expectation is a quasi-Monte-Carlo average over N draws from SobolQMCNormalSampler(num_samples=N, collapse_batch_dims=True, seed=seed) with N = 512 if |scope| <= 10000, 256 if <= 50000, 128 if <= 100000, else 64. Reference point r: r_i = min over observed (scaled, sign-flipped) y_i, unless objective_thresholds given, in which case thresholds are sign-flipped and passed through the y-scaler. If M == 1 EDBO+ silently switches to botorch qExpectedImprovement(best_f = max(y_std)) with the same sampler ('EHVI' option similarly uses qExpectedHypervolumeImprovement with NondominatedPartitioning). Batch of q points: optimize_acqf_discrete(acq_function, choices = scaled tensor of all PENDING rows, q = batch, unique=True) — botorch selects the q points sequentially, adding each choice to X_pending so joint (fantasy-aware) MC values are used; chosen scaled vectors are mapped back to scope rows by nearest neighbor under cityblock (L1) distance and given priority=1 (measured rows get priority=-1).

EDBO+ round-0 initialization (no measured rows): default init_sampling_method='cvt' — Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation 'selection' sampling over the one-hot-encoded scope matrix (idaes pysmo CVTSampling); options 'lhs' (LatinHypercubeSampling, selection mode) and 'random' (pandas .sample with seed); shortfalls topped up with seeded random rows; selected rows marked priority=1 in the CSV. edbo init_method options: 'rand' (default), k-means/PAM clustering via pyclustering, 'external'.

EDBO+ end-to-end round algorithm (run()): (1) read scope CSV; rows with 'PENDING' in any objective column = candidate/test set, fully measured rows = training set; (2) one-hot-encode non-numeric columns (pd.get_dummies, drop_first=True), numeric columns pass through; (3) if no training rows: do init sampling, write priority column, return; (4) fit M GPs as above; (5) optimize qNEHVI over candidates for q=batch points; (6) posterior-predict mean/var for EVERY scope row in chunks of ~1000, inverse-transform, compute raw-scale EI diagnostics; (7) write pred_<filename>.csv (with <obj>_predicted_mean, <obj>_predicted_std_dev, <obj>_expected_improvement per objective) and rewrite <filename>.csv sorted by priority. Global seeding: torch.manual_seed(seed), np.random.seed(seed) at the top of every run.
design_recommendations: Do NOT take edbo or edboplus as a hard dependency of the framework. edbo is dead code on modern Python (3.7.5 + gpytorch 1.0.0 + pyro-ppl 1.1); edboplus only runs in a Python 3.9 env with botorch==0.5.0/gpytorch==1.5.1/torch==1.10.0/idaes-pse==1.5.1 and breaks on current botorch (botorch.sampling.samplers and the num_samples= sampler signature were removed in botorch >=0.8) and current idaes (idaes.surrogate -> idaes.core.surrogate). Instead ship (a) a first-class backend written against CURRENT botorch/gpytorch that replicates EDBO+'s model exactly, and (b) an optional 'genuine EDBO+' adapter that shells out to an isolated Python 3.9 venv/conda env via the CSV interface, for cross-validation of suggestions.

Adapter interface (protocol class, e.g. optimizers/base.py): class BOBackend(Protocol): fit(X: np.ndarray | pd.DataFrame, Y: np.ndarray, objective_modes: list[str]) -> None; predict(X) -> tuple[mean: (N,M) array, std: (N,M) array]  # raw units, for chained-GP uncertainty propagation; suggest(candidates: pd.DataFrame, batch_size: int, exclude: pd.DataFrame | None) -> pd.DataFrame  # rows drawn from candidates; plus attributes/diagnostics: per-candidate acquisition values, ref_point, seed. Implementations: BoTorchEDBOBackend (native replica), EDBOplusSubprocessBackend (writes scope CSV with PENDING rows + measured rows, invokes EDBOplus().run in the pinned env, parses 'priority'==1 rows and pred_*.csv back), SklearnGPBackend / GPyGPBackend (fallbacks). Because every backend consumes a discrete candidate DataFrame, the simplex handling lives OUTSIDE the backends in one place.

Search space for the metal-fraction simplex: both EDBO packages require an enumerated candidate list, so generate a candidate DataFrame each round — e.g. a simplex lattice (all compositions with fractions in {0, 1/k, ..., 1} summing to 1, k~50-100 for 3-4 metals, i.e. 10^3-10^5 rows) optionally densified near the current Pareto/best points, or ~2*10^4 Dirichlet(alpha=1) samples. This makes the sum-to-1 constraint trivial (enforced at candidate construction) and matches optimize_acqf_discrete semantics. Keep metal fractions as numeric columns (they will NOT be one-hot encoded); zeolite support type, if varied, enters as a categorical column and gets OHE'd exactly as EDBO+ does (pd.get_dummies, drop_first=True).

Fallback GP spec to replicate for behavior parity when edbo is not installed (this is the exact recipe to freeze in code + docs): inputs MinMax-scaled to [0,1] per feature (fit scaler on training rows only); each objective sign-flipped for minimization then standardized to zero-mean/unit-variance (std floor 1e-6); model = ConstantMean + ScaleKernel(MaternKernel(nu=2.5, ard_num_dims=D, lengthscale_prior=GammaPrior(2.0, 0.2))) with outputscale_prior=GammaPrior(5.0, 0.5), GaussianLikelihood(noise_prior=GammaPrior(1.5, 0.1)), initial values lengthscale=5.0 (all dims), outputscale=8.0, noise=5.0, raw-noise constraint GreaterThan(1e-5), dtype float64; fit by Adam(lr=0.1) on -ExactMarginalLogLikelihood for 1000 iterations (EDBO+ numbers; edbo used 100 iters + optional restarts). NOTE for our low-D composition space: edbo's own BO_express would instead pick the low-D priors (lengthscale GammaPrior(1.2, 1.1) init 0.2, outputscale GammaPrior(5.0, 0.5) init 8.0, noise GammaPrior(1.05, 0.5) init 0.1) for <5 features — expose 'edboplus_default' and 'edbo_lowdim' as named prior presets and benchmark both on our data; with 3-4 MinMax-scaled composition features the low-D preset is the better-motivated default.

GPy fallback can be made near-equivalent because GPy supports MAP with Gamma priors (same shape/rate convention): kern = GPy.kern.Matern52(input_dim=D, ARD=True); kern.lengthscale.set_prior(GPy.priors.Gamma(2.0, 0.2)); kern.variance.set_prior(GPy.priors.Gamma(5.0, 0.5)); model.likelihood.variance.set_prior(GPy.priors.Gamma(1.5, 0.1)); set the same initial values and a 1e-5 lower bound on likelihood variance; optimize with model.optimize(). scikit-learn's GaussianProcessRegressor CANNOT encode hyperpriors (only kernel hyperparameter bounds + n_restarts_optimizer, ML-II not MAP); if sklearn is the only available backend use kernel = ConstantKernel(8.0) * Matern(length_scale=[5.0]*D, nu=2.5) + WhiteKernel(5.0, noise_level_bounds=(1e-5, 1e5)), normalize_y=True, n_restarts_optimizer>=8, and document loudly that suggestions will diverge from EDBO in the small-data regime where priors matter most (first 2-4 rounds of 6).

Batch strategy for our 6 suggestions/round: single-FOM (integral of CH4 curve) -> either (a) EDBO-faithful: EI (xi=0.01 on standardized y) + Kriging believer with hyperparameter refit per fantasy (6 refits — cheap at our data sizes of tens of points), or (b) EDBO+-faithful: MC qEI (better joint behavior, one call) — implement (b) as default with (a) available for reproduction studies. Multi-objective (e.g. maximize CH4 FOM while minimizing CO or light-off T50) -> qNEHVI with ref_point = per-objective observed minimum unless the chemist supplies thresholds (map 'worst acceptable CH4 integral' / 'worst acceptable CO' through the same sign-flip + y-scaler as EDBO+ does). Always pass unique=True / dedup against measured compositions, and seed torch+numpy per round for reproducible suggestions.

Selected vs actual composition: EDBO has no concept of input noise. Follow its structure but train the GPs on the MEASURED (actual) metal fractions while running acquisition over the INTENDED candidate grid — this is exactly consistent with EDBO+'s design (train X and candidate X are just different row sets of the same feature space) and requires no adapter change. If input-noise modeling is later needed, that is a reason to prefer our native backend (e.g. add expected lengthscale inflation or a NoisyGP), not the EDBO packages.

Replicate EDBO+'s reporting pattern as framework diagnostics: after each round, emit a per-candidate table with <objective>_predicted_mean, <objective>_predicted_std_dev (raw units via mean = mu_std*s + m, var = var_std*s^2), the acquisition value, and the chosen batch flagged priority=1 / measured rows priority=-1. This gives chemists the same artifact EDBO+ users expect and doubles as the uncertainty-propagation input for the chained GP layer (curve-fit parameter GPs -> FOM GP).

Replace EDBO+'s idaes-pse dependency for round-0 design: implement 'random', 'lhs' and 'cvt' init over the encoded candidate matrix using scipy.stats.qmc.LatinHypercube + nearest-candidate snapping and k-means centroids + nearest-candidate snapping (k-means IS CVT selection in practice). Keep the same semantics: init only when zero measured rows exist, size = batch (6), seeded.

Version/compat guardrails in the EDBOplusSubprocessBackend: detect at import that the pinned env exists (python 3.9, botorch==0.5.0, gpytorch==1.5.1, torch==1.10.0, idaes-pse==1.5.1, numpy==1.21.5, pandas==1.3.4); never install these into the main framework env (namespace hazard: the edboplus repo installs a package literally named 'edbo', colliding with PyPI edbo 0.1.0). Communicate via files only: write reaction.csv scope, run `env/bin/python -c "from edbo.plus.optimizer_botorch import EDBOplus; EDBOplus().run(...)"`, read back priority + pred CSVs.

GammaPrior(a, b) in gpytorch is shape/rate (mean a/b); note the EDBO+ noise prior Gamma(1.5, 0.1) has mean 15 ON STANDARDIZED targets — it is a weak prior whose influence fades quickly with data, but it (plus init noise=5.0) biases very-small-data fits toward high noise/smooth means; expect first-round predictions to be conservative.

EDBO's Kriging believer refits GP hyperparameters after every fantasy point; with lie = posterior mean it can over-exploit (cluster batch points) on flat posteriors, and behavior depends on ADAM convergence (100 iters, no restarts by default) — replication of exact suggested batches also requires matching torch versions/seeds, which is generally NOT achievable bit-for-bit across torch releases; aim for statistical, not exact, parity.

The EI columns EDBO+ writes to pred_*.csv are computed on raw scale from raw best-observed values and are DIAGNOSTIC ONLY — the optimized acquisition is qNEHVI/qEI on standardized scale. Do not validate a reimplementation against those columns.

qNEHVI's default reference point (per-objective minimum of observed scaled values) makes early-round hypervolume rankings sensitive to the worst observation so far; supplying explicit objective_thresholds (worst acceptable FOM values) is more stable and is supported by both EDBO+ and our proposed adapter.

EDBO+'s nearest-candidate matching (cityblock argmin) after optimize_acqf_discrete is a no-op when candidates are passed exactly, but its OHE with drop_first=True means categorical distance is asymmetric for the dropped level — irrelevant for pure-numeric composition spaces, relevant if we add zeolite type as a categorical.

Benchmark context for expectations: EDBO was validated on a 1728-configuration Pd direct-arylation space (12 ligands x 4 bases x 4 solvents x 3 temperatures x 3 concentrations, sources differ on the 4-solvent/3-solvent split but total = 1728) plus Mitsunobu and deoxyfluorination campaigns, all with categorical-heavy chemistry descriptor spaces (DFT/Mordred/OHE); EDBO+ on a 1728-configuration Ni/photoredox cross-electrophile coupling optimizing yield + ee in 15-24 experiments. Neither was validated on low-dimensional continuous composition simplexes like ours — the low-D prior preset exists in edbo's code but was not the headline-validated configuration, so run our own retrospective benchmarks before trusting either preset.

schoenebeck.summary:
The publication that matches "Schoenebeck noisy-data augmentation" is Hueffel, J. A.; Bindschaedler, Q. P.; Sala, F.; Schoenebeck, F. "Empowering Reactivity Predictions through Noise-Based Data Augmentation", J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2025, 147 (36), 33232-33239 (DOI 10.1021/jacs.5c11632; RWTH Aachen). It is the group's only noise-augmentation paper; the earlier ML papers the prompt hints at (Karl, T. M. et al., JACS 2023, 145, 15414 - Ni(I) dimers; Hueffel et al., Science 2021, 374, 1134 - Pd(I) dimers; the Ni(I)/CO2-insertion paper JACS 2025, DOI 10.1021/jacs.5c00441) use unsupervised/assumption-based ML with NO noise augmentation (verified by grepping their code repos: zero hits for noise/augment). No Schoenebeck co-author "Emme" exists; that hint appears misremembered. The official implementation is the AIxChem pipeline at github.com/Schoenebeck-Lab/Augmentation (cloned locally to /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-YARP/0d9d4afc-ded1-584b-98fd-0f24d7349d4e/scratchpad/Augmentation; algorithm in aixchem/transform/augment.py, split handling in aixchem/pipeline/pipe.py, worked configs in docs/leitch/aug_AGN_RF.py and the repo wiki). Note the ACS full text/SI is paywalled and was unreachable through this session's proxy, so the algorithm below is reconstructed from the authors' own code, repo wiki, results workbooks, and abstract - the code is authoritative and complete.

The exact algorithm ("AGN", AdditiveGaussianNoise): after z-score standardization of descriptors (scaler fit on the training fold only), each training point is replicated n times and each replica is perturbed with i.i.d. element-wise Gaussian noise N(mu=0, sigma^2). Noise is ALWAYS considered for the inputs X (transform_X=True default) and OPTIONALLY for the targets y (transform_y in {False, True} is itself grid-searched); the augmented training set is the union of the original N points plus n noisy replicas, size (n+1)N. Constructor defaults are mu=0, sigma=0.5, n=1, transform_y=False; in the paper's experiments sigma in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5} (X-noise in standardized SD units; y-noise in raw target units because their Scaler does not scale y) and n in {1..5} (up to 10-20 for tiny 5-10% training fractions) are tuned by grid search. Critically, augmentation is applied ONLY to training data after splitting: their Pipeline.run_sequence explicitly skips Augmenter steps for test/holdout sets ("augmentation should only be applied to training data"), and all metrics are computed on original, un-augmented points. Their evaluation protocol: RepeatedKFold(n_splits=4, n_repeats=5) => 20 folds with 25% holdout each; step 1 optimizes model hyperparameters without augmentation; step 2 fixes those and grid-searches (n, sigma, transform_y) against a no-augmentation control on identical folds, selecting by mean holdout RMSE; significance via one-tailed paired t-test and a two-step TOST equivalence test. Counter-controls in the code isolate the mechanism: DuplicateData (exact copies, no noise) and AGN_Y_Shuffler (noisy X with shuffled y) - benefit must come from noise, not dataset inflation.

Scope and reported benefits: benchmarked on 5 literature reactivity datasets - SNAr experimental activation energies (443 rxns, Jorner/Buttar/Norrby), Pd oxidative-addition Delta-G (74 aryl halides, Leitch), CPA-iminium enantioselectivity (~367 rxns, Sigman), asymmetric-hydrogenation ee (~368 rxns, Sunoj), and Buchwald-Hartwig HTE yields (3955 rxns, Doyle) - with MLR, kNN, RF and MLP models. From the repo's results workbooks: gains are largest in low-data regimes (e.g., SNAr at 5% training: MLR MAE 4.41->2.32; Sigman ee, RF MAE 0.79->0.70 with p<0.001 at every fraction; Doyle yields at 20%: MLP MAE 9.35->8.20 with p<0.001, while RF gains there were small and non-significant - benefits are model- and dataset-dependent). TOST analysis on SNAr showed 60% of the data + AGN is statistically equivalent to 90% without augmentation, i.e. ~30% fewer experiments (99 reactions saved). AGN matched or beat far costlier generators (NN-SMOTE interpolation, TVAE, CTGAN) and runs in under a second. Prior art you should co-cite: Cortes-Ciriano & Bender (JCIM 2015) introduced essentially the same replicate+Gaussian-noise scheme for QSAR (noise on responses, descriptors, both, or neither); Schoenebeck's contribution is the systematic demonstration on small experimental reactivity/selectivity/yield datasets plus the rigorous statistical selection protocol. Importantly for your GP-chained framework: in their method sigma is a TUNED hyperparameter, not fixed to the experimental error - but tying sigma_y to replicate-derived noise is the natural principled default (see recommendations).
key_equations_or_algorithms: AGN augmentation (core, from aixchem/transform/augment.py AdditiveGaussianNoise): Given training set D_train = {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1..N}, x_i in R^d (z-score standardized per feature, scaler fit on training fold only), y_i in R^m (raw units). Augmented set D_aug = D_train UNION union_{j=1..n} { (x_i + eps_ij, y_i + delta_ij) : i=1..N }, where eps_ij ~ N(mu * 1_d, sigma^2 * I_d) drawn i.i.d. element-wise, and delta_ij ~ N(mu, sigma^2 * I_m) if transform_y=True else delta_ij = 0. Variables: n = number of noisy replicas of the FULL training set (so |D_aug| = (n+1) * N); mu = noise mean (always 0); sigma = noise standard deviation (same scalar applied to all X columns in standardized units and, if enabled, to y in raw units). Code defaults: mu=0, sigma=0.5, n=1, transform_X=True, transform_y=False. Paper grids: sigma in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5}; transform_y in {False, True}; n in {1,2,3,4,5} for training fractions >= 30%, up to {1..10} at 10% and {1..20} at 5% (smaller data -> more replicas allowed).

Full training/evaluation protocol (pseudocode, faithful to their Pipeline + docs/leitch/aug_AGN_RF.py):
for (dev, holdout) in RepeatedKFold(n_splits=4, n_repeats=5, seed).split(data):   # 20 outer folds, holdout = 25%
    (train, test) = simple_split(dev, train_size=f)                               # f = data-availability fraction being simulated; omit for full data
    scaler = StandardScaler().fit(train.X); apply to train.X, test.X, holdout.X   # y NOT scaled
    for cfg in GRID over {None} UNION {(n, sigma, transform_y)}:                  # 'None' = un-augmented control
        train_aug = AGN(cfg).transform(train)      # ONLY the training set is augmented; test/holdout NEVER augmented
        model = Model(fixed_hyperparams_from_step1).fit(train_aug.X, train_aug.y)
        record RMSE/MAE/R2 of model on train, test, holdout (original points only)
select cfg* = argmin over cfg of mean holdout RMSE across the 20 folds
Step 1 (done beforehand, identical loop without augmentation): grid-search model hyperparameters (e.g., RF n_estimators in {100,200,500,1000,2000}, max_depth in {None,10,20}) and fix the best per condition.

Statistical validation: (a) one-tailed paired t-test comparing the per-fold holdout metric of augmented vs non-augmented models over the K=20 folds; improvement claimed when p < 0.05 (most reported cases p < 0.01 or < 0.001). (b) Two-step TOST (two one-sided tests) equivalence procedure: step 1 - find the smallest un-augmented training fraction f* whose holdout RMSE distribution is statistically equivalent to using 100% of the data (on SNAr: f* = 90%); step 2 - find the smallest AUGMENTED fraction f_aug equivalent to f* un-augmented (on SNAr: f_aug = 60%); data saving = (f* - f_aug) * N_total (SNAr: 0.30 * 0.75 * 443 ~= 99 reactions).

Counter-controls (implement as sanity checks): (1) DuplicateData: append n exact copies of the training set (no noise) - tests whether gains are mere dataset inflation (they are not); (2) AGN_Y_Shuffler: add Gaussian noise to X replicas but randomly permute their y values - destroys the X-y mapping; a model exploiting real structure must get worse. A useful acceptance test: RMSE(AGN) < RMSE(none) ~= RMSE(duplicate) << RMSE(y-shuffle) is the expected ordering.

Recommended sigma when experimental noise is known/estimable (our synthesis; in the paper sigma is purely tuned): (a) From R replicate measurements of each condition k: sigma_y^2 = sum_k sum_r (y_kr - ybar_k)^2 / sum_k (R_k - 1) (pooled replicate variance, in raw y units - directly usable since their pipeline leaves y unscaled). (b) From kinetic-fit residuals when replicates are unavailable: sigma_curve^2 ~= RSS / (T - p), where RSS = sum over the T temperature points of squared residuals of the fitted light-off curve and p = number of kinetic parameters; propagate to an integral FOM F = integral of c_CH4(T) dT via the delta method: sigma_F^2 = g^T Cov(theta_hat) g with g = dF/dtheta evaluated at the fit optimum, Cov(theta_hat) = sigma_curve^2 * (J^T J)^{-1}, J = Jacobian of the model curve w.r.t. kinetic parameters theta. (c) For X-noise on compositions: sigma_x,j = SD over past runs of (x_measured,j - x_selected,j) for metal fraction j (this is exactly your measured-vs-selected discrepancy); to use in standardized units divide by the training-fold SD of the feature. (d) If tuning instead, keep their grid sigma in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5} (standardized units), n in {1..5} for N >~ 100, n up to 10-20 for N < ~30 - and confirm selection with the paired t-test.

Simplex-respecting input noise for metal fractions (our adaptation - naive AGN breaks sum-to-one): either (i) jitter-and-project: x' = clip(x + eps, 0, 1); x' = x' / sum(x'); or (ii) jitter in isometric log-ratio space: z = ILR(x), z' = z + N(0, sigma_z^2 I_{d-1}), x' = ILR^{-1}(z'), which stays strictly inside the simplex; or (iii) draw x' ~ Dirichlet(x / s) with concentration s calibrated so SD matches the composition-measurement error.
design_recommendations: Implement AGN as a train-fold-only transformer with the exact semantics of their code: augment AFTER (a) train/test/holdout splitting and (b) feature standardization fit on the training fold; never augment validation/test/holdout data; compute all metrics on original points only. If you ever pre-augment before splitting, enforce GroupKFold with the parent-point ID as the group so all copies of a point live in one fold (their pipeline avoids leakage by construction; replicate that guarantee with an assertion/unit test).

API sketch mirroring theirs: AGNAugmenter(n=3, sigma=0.1, mu=0.0, noise_on_X=True, noise_on_y=False, sigma_y=None, random_state=None).fit_resample(X, y) -> (X_aug, y_aug) of size (n+1)N, with an index/flag marking augmented rows (they suffix the index with '*') so downstream code can drop them for evaluation. Support per-column sigma vectors so composition noise (from measured-vs-selected discrepancy) and target noise (from replicate/fit-residual error) can differ.

Default hyperparameter policy: if replicate or fit-residual noise estimates exist, set sigma_y = that estimate (raw units) and sigma_x = per-feature measurement SD (standardized), with n=3; otherwise grid-search sigma in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5}, n in {1..5} (allow up to 10-20 when N_train < ~30, i.e., your first 2-5 AL rounds of 6 points), noise_on_y in {False, True}, selected by mean holdout RMSE over repeated k-fold (their choice: 4-fold x 5 repeats) and accepted only if a one-tailed paired t-test vs the no-augmentation control gives p < 0.05.

Where to use it in your stack: AGN's demonstrated wins are for non-Bayesian learners (MLR, MLP, kNN, RF) in low-data regimes - so apply it to your RF/GBM baselines and any neural kinetic-parameter surrogates, and to the kinetic-curve-fitting-to-FOM regressors. It is largely REDUNDANT for exact GPs on the target side: a GP already models Gaussian target noise via WhiteKernel/alpha, and n replicas of identical X with noisy y roughly reproduce what alpha does while inflating cost from O(N^3) to O((n+1)^3 N^3). For your chained GPs, prefer (a) heteroscedastic per-point alpha_i = sigma_i^2 with sigma_i from the kinetic-fit covariance of each point's FOM, and (b) AGN-style INPUT jitter (or NIGP/expected-kernel methods) to propagate measured-composition uncertainty - input noise is the component a standard GP cannot natively absorb.

For composition (simplex) inputs, never add raw Gaussian noise: jitter in ILR space or renormalize after clipping (see equations); calibrate sigma_x from your measured-vs-selected composition history - this doubles as an empirical noise model for the selected->measured composition GP link in your chain.

Ship their two counter-controls (DuplicateData, y-shuffled AGN) as built-in diagnostics and CI tests: augmentation is only enabled by default when AGN significantly beats both the no-aug control and the duplication control on repeated CV (paired t-test), mirroring the paper's validation logic; optionally add their two-step TOST to quantify 'experiments saved', a compelling metric for your reports.

Keep augmentation OUT of the BO acquisition loop's uncertainty quantification unless done consistently: if a surrogate is trained on augmented data, its predictive variance no longer reflects N real points; for the 6-points-per-round batch BO, fit the acquisition GP on real points with noise encoded via alpha, and use AGN only for auxiliary/deterministic predictors. Log the augmentation config (n, sigma, seed) with every model artifact for reproducibility - their code seeds numpy per transform.
