bo_gp.summary:
(1) Simplex handling. The metal-fraction design space is the (d-1)-simplex Delta = {x in R^d : x_i >= 0, sum_i x_i = 1}. Three workable representations exist: (a) raw fractions with a standard kernel — valid because any positive-definite kernel on R^d restricted to the simplex remains valid; this is the recommended default because it tolerates zero fractions (pure/absent metals), which log-ratio transforms cannot; (b) additive log-ratio (alr) and isometric log-ratio (ilr) transforms from Aitchison compositional-data analysis (Egozcue et al. 2003), which map the open simplex bijectively to R^(d-1) so the GP and acquisition optimizer see an unconstrained Euclidean space — ilr is isometric (distance-preserving w.r.t. Aitchison geometry) and preferred over alr, but both diverge at the boundary and require pseudo-count replacement of zeros; (c) exotic simplex-native approaches (Wasserstein-distance GPs, Candelieri et al. 2024) that only pay off at high d. Uniform simplex sampling is Dirichlet(1,...,1) via normalized Gamma/Exponential draws; acquisition optimization on the simplex is done robustly at d <= ~6 by dense Dirichlet candidate sets (global Dir(1) + local Dir(kappa*x_best) clouds) followed by SLSQP polishing with the equality constraint, or by unconstrained optimization in softmax/ilr coordinates. Initial designs should combine a Scheffe-type simplex lattice (vertices, edge midpoints, centroid) with maximin-subsampled Dirichlet points.

(2) GP practice at 10-200 points. Use Matern 5/2 with ARD lengthscales as default (standard recommendation since Snoek et al. 2012 — RBF's infinite smoothness is unrealistic for physical responses and yields overconfident extrapolation); fit by maximizing the log marginal likelihood with L-BFGS-B on log-hyperparameters and 10-20 random restarts. MLE for GP hyperparameters is formally ill-posed (Karvonen & Oates, JMLR 2023) and small-n fits routinely degenerate to lengthscale -> 0 (interpolation, noise absorbed into signal) or lengthscale -> infinity (constant/linear mean); the fixes are hard bounds after scaling inputs (lengthscale in ~[0.05, 5] on a unit-scaled simplex) plus, ideally, lognormal or inverse-gamma priors turning MLE into MAP (Stan guidance). Standardize y (zero mean, unit variance) and bound the signal variance near 1. Heteroscedastic known noise enters scikit-learn via a per-point alpha vector added to the kernel diagonal — with the critical caveat that alpha lives in the (internally standardized) y units, so known physical noise variances must be divided by Var(y); manual standardization is safer. Per-point noise variances should come from the curve-fitting stage (parameter covariance propagated to the figure of merit) and/or replicates. With n < ~10*d, prefer an isotropic kernel and switch to ARD as data accumulates.

(3) Batch acquisition (q ~ 6) and (4) chained models. Four batch strategies are implementable without BoTorch, in increasing complexity: constant liar / Kriging believer (Ginsbourger et al. 2010) — greedy loop appending fake observations (lie = best/worst/mean observed for CL, posterior mean for KB) and refitting WITHOUT re-optimizing hyperparameters; local penalization (Gonzalez et al., AISTATS 2016) — multiply the acquisition by Lipschitz-based exclusion-ball penalizers around already-chosen points, no refits at all; Monte-Carlo q-EI (Ginsbourger; Wilson et al., NeurIPS 2018) — joint-posterior sampling via Cholesky with fixed base samples, optimized greedily one point at a time (greedy is near-optimal by submodularity); and batch Thompson sampling (Kandasamy et al. 2018; Hernandez-Lobato et al. 2017) via random-Fourier-feature posterior sample paths, each maximized independently. Empirical comparisons in materials contexts (Mia et al., Digital Discovery 2025) find MC batch acquisitions (qEI/qUCB) more robust under observation noise and less sensitive to initialization than serial UCB+LP, while both perform well noiselessly; for a 6-point noisy experimental campaign, greedy MC-qEI with a CL fallback and one pure-exploration/TS hedge point is a defensible default. Because the pipeline is composition -> (measured composition, kinetic-curve parameters) -> FOM with the last map g known and cheap, composite-function BO (Astudillo & Frazier, ICML 2019: EI-CF, sampling the intermediate GP posterior and pushing samples through g) is markedly more sample-efficient than a GP directly on the FOM. Uncertainty propagation through the chain: default to Monte Carlo (draw from stage-1 posterior, evaluate stage-2 predictive at each draw, combine via the law of total variance, ~1000-4000 samples is trivial for GP predictives); the delta method (first/second-order Taylor) is the fast linearized alternative but is unreliable through strongly nonlinear stages such as sigmoidal light-off curves; analytic moment-matching through GP chains exists for Matern kernels (linked GPs, Ming & Guillas, SIAM/ASA JUQ 2021) and full variational treatment is Deep/Chained GPs (Damianou & Lawrence 2013; Saul et al. 2016) — both cited as upgrades, not v1 requirements. Input noise from measured-vs-selected composition can be absorbed with the NIGP trick (McHutchon & Rasmussen 2011): inflate output noise by the squared posterior-mean slope times the input-noise covariance.

(5) Validation. Every refit should report leave-one-out metrics computed from the closed-form GP LOO identities (Rasmussen & Williams GPML eqs. 5.10-5.12; O(n^3) once, no refits): LOO-RMSE, negative log predictive density (NLPD), 95%-interval coverage, and the variance of standardized LOO residuals (z-scores) — z-variance >> 1 means overconfident (widen noise/lengthscale bounds), << 1 underconfident. Reliability diagrams and isotonic recalibration follow Kuleshov et al. (ICML 2018); for a BO surrogate the pragmatic version is a single scalar variance-rescaling factor s = std(z) applied to predictive sigmas when calibration drifts outside ~[0.7, 1.3]. Coverage estimates on n ~ 20 points carry large binomial error and should be tracked as trends across rounds rather than gated per-round.
key_equations_or_algorithms: SIMPLEX AND DIRICHLET SAMPLING. Design space: Delta^(d-1) = {x in R^d : x_i >= 0, sum_{i=1..d} x_i = 1}, d = number of metals. Uniform sampling: draw e_i ~ Exponential(1) (or g_i ~ Gamma(alpha_i,1) for general Dirichlet(alpha)), set x_i = e_i / sum_j e_j; alpha = (1,...,1) gives the uniform distribution on the simplex. Local sampling around a point x0 (for acquisition polishing / batch diversity): x ~ Dirichlet(kappa * (x0 + eps_floor)) with concentration kappa ~ 50-500 (mean ~= x0, spread shrinks as kappa grows) and eps_floor ~ 1e-3 so zero components can still move. Initial design recipe: (i) simplex-lattice points {vertices, edge midpoints, centroid} (Scheffe mixture design), (ii) top up with greedy maximin selection from ~10^4 uniform Dirichlet draws: repeatedly add the candidate maximizing min distance to already-chosen points.

LOG-RATIO TRANSFORMS (Aitchison; Egozcue et al. 2003). alr: z_i = ln(x_i / x_d), i = 1..d-1; inverse x_i = exp(z_i)/(1 + sum_j exp(z_j)) for i<d, x_d = 1/(1 + sum_j exp(z_j)). Not isometric (depends on reference component d). clr: clr(x)_i = ln(x_i / g(x)), g(x) = (prod_j x_j)^(1/d) (geometric mean); clr coordinates sum to 0 (rank d-1). ilr: z = V^T clr(x), where V is d x (d-1) with orthonormal columns spanning {v : 1^T v = 0} (V^T V = I_{d-1}); pivot-coordinate construction: z_j = sqrt(j/(j+1)) * ln( g(x_1..x_j) / x_{j+1} ), j = 1..d-1. Inverse: clr = V z, x = softmax(clr). ilr is an isometry between (Delta, Aitchison metric) and R^(d-1) — GP + optimizer become fully unconstrained. Zero handling (mandatory before alr/ilr): multiplicative replacement x_i=0 -> delta (e.g. delta = 1e-3), rescale nonzero parts by (1 - n_zeros*delta). If the campaign includes pure metals or deliberate zero fractions, do NOT use log-ratios; fit the GP on raw fractions instead.

ACQUISITION OPTIMIZATION ON THE SIMPLEX (recipe, d <= ~6). Step 1: evaluate acquisition alpha(x) on N_g ~ 10000 uniform Dirichlet candidates + N_l ~ 1000 local candidates Dirichlet(kappa*(x_best_observed + eps)) + all previously measured points perturbed. Step 2: take the top-k (k ~ 10) candidates and polish each with scipy.optimize.minimize(method='SLSQP', fun = -alpha, bounds = [(0,1)]*d, constraints = [{'type':'eq', 'fun': lambda x: x.sum() - 1}]). Step 3: return the best polished point. Alternative unconstrained parameterization: x = softmax(t) with t_d fixed at 0 (removes shift degeneracy), optimize over t in R^(d-1) with L-BFGS multi-start; or optimize in ilr coordinates. For projected-gradient variants, Euclidean projection onto the simplex is the O(d log d) sort-and-threshold algorithm of Duchi et al. (ICML 2008): sort x descending, find rho = max{j : x_(j) - (cumsum_j - 1)/j > 0}, theta = (cumsum_rho - 1)/rho, output max(x_i - theta, 0).

MATERN 5/2 ARD KERNEL. k(x, x') = sigma_f^2 * (1 + sqrt(5) r + (5/3) r^2) * exp(-sqrt(5) r), with r^2 = sum_{i=1..d} (x_i - x'_i)^2 / l_i^2; sigma_f^2 = signal variance, l_i = per-dimension (ARD) lengthscales. Sample paths are twice differentiable — smooth enough for kinetic responses, rougher than RBF (whose C-infinity paths cause overconfident long-range extrapolation on small physical datasets). On the simplex the d inputs are linearly dependent (sum = 1), so ARD lengthscales are identifiable only up to that constraint — acceptable in practice; alternatively drop one component or use ilr coordinates for a full-rank input.

MARGINAL-LIKELIHOOD FITTING WITH RESTARTS AND GUARDS. Objective: log p(y|X,theta) = -1/2 y^T K_y^{-1} y - 1/2 log|K_y| - n/2 log(2*pi), K_y = K_theta + diag(alpha_1..alpha_n) (+ sigma_n^2 I if a learned WhiteKernel is included), theta = {sigma_f, l_1..l_d, sigma_n} optimized in log-space with L-BFGS-B. Algorithm: (1) scale inputs (simplex already in [0,1]); standardize outputs y <- (y - mean(y))/std(y); (2) set bounds: l_i in [0.05, 5.0] (lower bound ~ half the minimum expected nearest-neighbor spacing; upper ~ 5x domain diameter), sigma_f^2 in [0.1, 20], sigma_n^2 in [1e-6, 1.0]; (3) run n_restarts = 10-20, first from a sensible init (l = 0.3, sigma_f = 1, sigma_n = 0.1), rest from log-uniform draws within bounds; keep the best LML; (4) degeneracy check: flag fits with any l_i at a bound or sigma_n^2 at its floor; (5) optional MAP instead of MLE: add log-prior sum_i log LogNormal(l_i; mu = log 0.3, s = 0.7) + log LogNormal(sigma_n; ...) to the objective (custom optimizer closure; scikit-learn supports custom optimizer= callables). Rationale: unpenalized MLE is ill-posed (Karvonen & Oates 2023) and small-n LML surfaces have flat ridges in lengthscale.

SCIKIT-LEARN SURROGATE SPEC WITH HETEROSCEDASTIC NOISE. kernel = ConstantKernel(1.0, (0.1, 20)) * Matern(length_scale = [0.3]*d, length_scale_bounds = (0.05, 5.0), nu = 2.5) + WhiteKernel(noise_level = 0.05, noise_level_bounds = (1e-6, 1.0)); gp = GaussianProcessRegressor(kernel = kernel, alpha = sigma_i_sq_std, n_restarts_optimizer = 15, normalize_y = False) where the package standardizes y itself: y_std = (y - m_y)/s_y, and per-point known noise variances (from the curve-fit stage) are passed as alpha_i = sigma_FOM_i^2 / s_y^2. Gotcha this avoids: with normalize_y = True, sklearn adds alpha to the kernel diagonal in the standardized-y space, so raw physical variances passed as alpha are silently wrong by a factor s_y^2. The WhiteKernel then captures residual noise beyond the known per-point floor; drop it (alpha only) if replicates fully characterize noise. Predictions are un-standardized: mu = m_y + s_y*mu_std, sigma = s_y*sigma_std.

MONTE-CARLO q-EI WITH FIXED BASE SAMPLES (maximization). Joint posterior at batch X = (x_1..x_q): Y ~ N(mu(X), Sigma(X)), Sigma = K(X,X) - K(X,D) K_y^{-1} K(D,X) (+ jitter 1e-10 I). Estimator: draw base samples Z = (z^(1)..z^(S)), z^(s) ~ N(0, I_q), ONCE per batch-selection round; C = cholesky(Sigma); Y^(s) = mu + C z^(s); qEI(X) ~= (1/S) sum_s max(0, max_{j=1..q} Y_j^(s) - f*), f* = best (noise-adjusted) observed value or max posterior mean at observed points. S = 128-512 suffices. Fixing Z (common random numbers) makes qEI(X) a deterministic, continuous function of X so candidate ranking and SLSQP polishing are stable (Wilson et al. 2018). GREEDY CONSTRUCTION (near-optimal by submodularity, Wilson et al. 2018): x_1 = argmax EI(x) (closed form: EI = sigma(x)*(u*Phi(u) + phi(u)), u = (mu(x) - f* - xi)/sigma(x)); for j = 2..q: x_j = argmax_x qEI({x_1..x_{j-1}, x}) with the fixed base samples — each step is a single d-dimensional simplex optimization (candidate set + polish). No gradients or autodiff needed.

CONSTANT LIAR / KRIGING BELIEVER (Ginsbourger et al. 2010), maximization convention. Input: fitted GP, data D, batch size q. For j = 1..q: (1) x_j = argmax_x EI(x | D_aug); (2) assign fake observation y_fake: KB: y_fake = mu(x_j) (posterior mean); CL-max: y_fake = max(y) (optimistic lie -> strong local repulsion, more explorative batches); CL-min: y_fake = min(y) (pessimistic lie -> allows clustering, more exploitative); CL-mean: y_fake = mean(y); (3) D_aug <- D_aug + {(x_j, y_fake)} and refit the GP WITH HYPERPARAMETERS FROZEN (recompute Cholesky only — re-optimizing on hallucinated data biases the fit). Return {x_1..x_q}. ~15 lines on top of any GP. KB risk: if the posterior mean is wrong in unexplored regions the batch can chase phantoms; CL-max is the usual robust default for maximization.

LOCAL PENALIZATION (Gonzalez et al., AISTATS 2016), maximization. Penalized acquisition after choosing x_1..x_{j-1}: alpha_j(x) = g(alpha(x)) * prod_{k<j} phi(x; x_k), g = softplus (ensures positivity). Penalizer = probability that x lies outside the exclusion ball around x_k: phi(x; x_k) = Phi( (L*||x - x_k||_2 - (M - mu(x_k))) / sigma(x_k) ), where Phi = standard normal CDF, M = max_i y_i (current best), mu(.), sigma(.) = GP posterior mean/sd, and L = Lipschitz estimate of the objective: L = max over a dense candidate grid of ||grad mu(x)|| (finite differences on the posterior mean are fine). Derivation: the ball radius rho_k = (M - f(x_k))/L is Gaussian under the posterior at x_k; phi = P(||x - x_k|| > rho_k). Algorithm: x_1 = argmax alpha; each subsequent point multiplies in one more penalizer; zero model refits, cost ~ q acquisition maximizations. Weakness: performance is sensitive to the L estimate (too small -> clustered batch, too large -> over-spread).

BATCH THOMPSON SAMPLING VIA RANDOM FOURIER FEATURES (Kandasamy et al. 2018; Hernandez-Lobato et al. 2017; Rahimi & Recht 2007). Approximate posterior sample paths: features phi_i(x) = sqrt(2 sigma_f^2 / m) * cos(w_i^T x + b_i), i = 1..m (m = 500-2000), b_i ~ U[0, 2pi], w_i drawn from the kernel's spectral density: RBF-ARD: w = diag(1/l) z, z ~ N(0, I_d); Matern-nu ARD: multivariate-t with 2*nu dof: w = diag(1/l) z / sqrt(u/(2*nu)), z ~ N(0,I_d), u ~ ChiSquared(2*nu) (2*nu = 5 for Matern 5/2). Bayesian linear model f(x) ~= phi(x)^T theta, prior theta ~ N(0, I_m): posterior theta | D ~ N(mu_theta, V), V = (Phi^T Phi / sigma_n^2 + I_m)^{-1}, mu_theta = V Phi^T y / sigma_n^2, Phi = n x m feature matrix (use per-point noise: Phi^T diag(1/alpha_i) Phi etc. for heteroscedastic). Batch: for s = 1..q draw theta_s = mu_theta + chol(V) zeta_s, maximize f_s(x) = phi(x)^T theta_s over the simplex (cheap, deterministic, differentiable) -> x_s. Dedupe: if min pairwise distance < delta_synth (composition control precision, e.g. 0.02), resample or perturb. Naturally diverse and embarrassingly parallel; more explorative than qEI.

MONTE-CARLO PROPAGATION THROUGH A CHAINED MODEL + LAW OF TOTAL VARIANCE. Pipeline stage 1: p(u | x) = N(mu_1(x), Sigma_1(x)) (e.g. GP from selected composition to measured composition and/or kinetic-curve parameters, multi-output = independent GPs per output as v1); stage 2: p(y | u) = N(mu_2(u), sigma_2^2(u)) (GP or known deterministic map). Algorithm: for s = 1..S (S = 1000-4000): u^(s) = mu_1(x) + chol(Sigma_1(x)) z^(s); y^(s) ~ N(mu_2(u^(s)), sigma_2^2(u^(s))) — or, for moments only, record m^(s) = mu_2(u^(s)), v^(s) = sigma_2^2(u^(s)). Outputs: E[y|x] ~= mean_s m^(s); Var[y|x] = E_u[sigma_2^2] + Var_u[mu_2] ~= mean_s v^(s) + var_s m^(s) (law of total variance — report the two terms separately: first = intrinsic stage-2 uncertainty, second = uncertainty inherited from stage 1); quantiles from the y^(s) sample. Deterministic final maps (FOM = g(curve params), g known) simply set v^(s) = 0, y^(s) = g(u^(s)).

DELTA-METHOD (LINEARIZED) PROPAGATION. First order: with u ~ N(mu_1, Sigma_1) and y = mu_2(u): E[y] ~= mu_2(mu_1); Var[y] ~= J Sigma_1 J^T + sigma_2^2(mu_1), where J = d mu_2 / d u evaluated at mu_1 (finite differences on the GP mean, or analytic for known g). Second-order mean correction: E[y] ~= mu_2(mu_1) + 1/2 * trace(H Sigma_1), H = Hessian of mu_2 at mu_1. Valid when Sigma_1 is small relative to the curvature scale of mu_2; FAILS for sigmoidal light-off responses when input uncertainty spans the transition region — use MC there (it is cheap anyway). Same formula gives FOM noise from curve fitting: Var(FOM) ~= grad_p(FOM)^T Sigma_p grad_p(FOM), Sigma_p = covariance of fitted kinetic parameters (from scipy.optimize.curve_fit pcov or bootstrap), FOM = integral over T of C_CH4(T; p) dT evaluated by quadrature — this feeds the per-point GP alpha.

COMPOSITE-FUNCTION EXPECTED IMPROVEMENT, EI-CF (Astudillo & Frazier, ICML 2019). When the objective is f(x) = g(h(x)) with h = expensive vector-valued black box (curve/kinetic parameters vs composition, modeled by a multi-output GP) and g = cheap known map (e.g. integral of the CH4 curve): EI-CF(x) = E[ max(0, g(h_post(x)) - g*) ], h_post(x) ~ N(mu_h(x), Sigma_h(x)), g* = best g(h) observed. MC estimator with fixed base samples: EI-CF(x) ~= (1/S) sum_s max(0, g(mu_h(x) + C_h(x) z^(s)) - g*), C_h = chol(Sigma_h). Batch version: combine with greedy qEI logic (joint samples across batch points) or with CL. This exploits the known structure of the FOM and dominates plain EI on a scalar-FOM GP in sample efficiency; it is the natural acquisition for the chained architecture.

INPUT-NOISE CORRECTION, NIGP (McHutchon & Rasmussen, NeurIPS 2011). When training inputs are noisy (measured composition x_meas = x_true + e, e ~ N(0, Sigma_x)): approximate by inflating output noise with the local slope: effective per-point noise alpha_i_eff = alpha_i + grad mu(x_i)^T Sigma_x grad mu(x_i), where grad mu = gradient of the GP posterior mean (finite differences). Iterate once or twice: fit -> compute slopes -> refit with inflated alpha. Cheap, uses only machinery already present (per-point alpha).

CLOSED-FORM LEAVE-ONE-OUT CV FOR GPs (GPML eqs. 5.10-5.12; Sundararajan & Keerthi 2001). With K_y = K + diag(alpha) and its inverse (or Cholesky) already computed: LOO predictive mean mu_{-i} = y_i - [K_y^{-1} y]_i / [K_y^{-1}]_{ii}; LOO predictive variance sigma_{-i}^2 = 1 / [K_y^{-1}]_{ii}. Cost: one O(n^3) factorization, no refits (hyperparameters held at the full-data optimum — slightly optimistic; for n < 30 optionally verify with true refit-per-fold LOO). Metrics: LOO-RMSE = sqrt(mean_i (y_i - mu_{-i})^2); NLPD = (1/n) sum_i [ 1/2 log(2 pi sigma_{-i}^2) + (y_i - mu_{-i})^2 / (2 sigma_{-i}^2) ] (lower is better; unlike RMSE it punishes overconfidence); compare against the trivial baseline NLPD of N(mean(y), var(y)).

CALIBRATION / COVERAGE DIAGNOSTICS AND RESCALING (Kuleshov et al., ICML 2018 + standard z-score checks). Standardized LOO residuals: z_i = (y_i - mu_{-i}) / sigma_{-i}; should be ~ N(0,1). Checks: (a) var(z) ~ 1 (var(z) >> 1 -> overconfident intervals; << 1 -> underconfident); (b) empirical coverage: cov(gamma) = (1/n) sum_i 1{ |z_i| <= Phi^{-1}((1+gamma)/2) } for gamma = 0.5, 0.8, 0.95 — compare to gamma (binomial CI: +/- sqrt(gamma(1-gamma)/n), i.e. very loose at n ~ 20); (c) reliability diagram: for p in {0.05,...,0.95} plot hat-c(p) = (1/n) sum_i 1{ Phi(z_i) <= p } vs p; calibration error = sum_p (hat-c(p) - p)^2. Recalibration: full Kuleshov = isotonic regression mapping predicted CDF values Phi(z_i) to empirical quantiles; pragmatic BO version = single variance-rescaling factor s = std(z), report sigma_cal = s * sigma when s outside [0.7, 1.3]. Track all metrics per BO round to detect surrogate degradation.
design_recommendations: Represent compositions as length-d numpy arrays with an explicit CompositionSpace class that validates x_i >= 0, |sum - 1| < tol, renormalizes measured compositions, and owns the samplers (uniform Dirichlet, local Dirichlet around a point, simplex-lattice + maximin initial design) and the Duchi simplex projection.

Default GP input = raw metal fractions (works with zero fractions at simplex vertices/edges); expose ilr as an optional, pluggable input transform for interior-only campaigns, with automatic multiplicative zero-replacement and a hard error if a composition has a zero and ilr is requested without a pseudo-count setting.

Standard surrogate: ConstantKernel * Matern(nu=2.5, ARD) + WhiteKernel in scikit-learn, n_restarts_optimizer >= 15, lengthscale bounds (0.05, 5.0) on the unit simplex, signal-variance bounds (0.1, 20), noise bounds (1e-6, 1.0). Standardize y in your own code (not normalize_y=True) so per-point alpha can be passed as physical FOM variances divided by std(y)^2 without unit confusion. Flag any hyperparameter that lands on a bound.
Use isotropic Matern for n < ~10*d and switch to ARD automatically once past that threshold; make the switch decision data-driven by comparing LOO NLPD of both variants each round.

Compute per-point FOM noise variances in the curve-fitting stage: propagate the kinetic-fit parameter covariance (curve_fit pcov, or a parametric bootstrap over residuals) through the FOM integral via the delta method or 1000-sample MC; feed these as the GP alpha vector. Where replicate syntheses exist, pool replicate variance into the same alpha.

Batch selection default: greedy Monte-Carlo qEI with fixed base samples (S ~ 256), optimized per point by 10k-candidate Dirichlet screening + SLSQP polish with the sum-to-one equality constraint; provide ConstantLiar (CL-max for maximization) and KrigingBeliever as cheap fallbacks sharing the same greedy-loop interface, and LocalPenalization and RFF-ThompsonSampling as alternative strategies behind a common BatchAcquisition ABC. Freeze hyperparameters during any fantasy/lie refits.

Hedge each 6-point batch: reserve 1 slot for pure exploration (max posterior sigma, or one Thompson sample) and fill 5 slots with the exploit-oriented strategy; enforce a minimum pairwise composition distance equal to the synthesis control precision (e.g. 0.02 absolute fraction) via rejection inside the greedy loop.

Implement the chained model as a ModelChain of stages each exposing predict_dist(x) -> (mean, cov); propagation defaults to MC with law-of-total-variance decomposition (report inherited vs intrinsic variance separately — this tells the user whether better composition control or more kinetic replicates reduces uncertainty faster); offer delta-method propagation as a fast option with an automatic warning when the second-order mean correction exceeds ~10% of the first-order variance.

Prefer composite-function BO over a direct FOM GP: model the fitted kinetic/curve parameters (or a low-dimensional curve summary) as independent GPs over composition, define the FOM as a deterministic function g of those parameters, and use MC EI-CF as the acquisition; keep the plain scalar-FOM GP + qEI as the simpler baseline mode for comparison.

Handle selected-vs-measured composition explicitly: train surrogates on measured compositions; when optimizing the acquisition (over selectable compositions), either assume identity mapping with input noise (NIGP-style alpha inflation using the estimated selected-to-measured error covariance) or fit a light 'controllability' GP from selected to measured composition as chain stage 0.

Ship a validation module run automatically after every refit: closed-form LOO (mu_{-i}, sigma_{-i}) from the single Cholesky factorization, reporting LOO-RMSE, NLPD (with the N(mean,var) trivial baseline), 50/80/95% coverage with binomial error bars, z-score variance, and a reliability-diagram array; log per-round to enable trend plots; apply optional scalar variance recalibration s = std(z) when |log s| > log(1.3).

Seed and record all stochastic elements (Dirichlet candidates, qEI base samples, RFF frequencies, restart initializations) so a batch proposal is exactly reproducible from (data, config, seed); this matters for an experimental campaign where proposals must be auditable.

Keep dependencies to numpy/scipy/scikit-learn as specified: everything above needs only cholesky/solve_triangular, scipy.stats.norm, scipy.optimize (L-BFGS-B, SLSQP), and sklearn.gaussian_process; do not pull in BoTorch/GPyTorch for d <= 6, n <= 200, q = 6.
caveats: Log-ratio (alr/ilr) transforms are undefined at the simplex boundary; pseudo-count zero replacement distorts geometry near vertices. Since single-metal and metal-absent formulations are chemically meaningful here, raw-fraction inputs should be the default and ilr strictly opt-in.

scikit-learn's GaussianProcessRegressor applies the per-point alpha in the internally standardized y-space when normalize_y=True; passing raw physical noise variances there is silently wrong by a factor Var(y). Standardize y manually.

GP hyperparameter MLE is ill-posed (Karvonen & Oates 2023): with 10-30 points, restarts can land on qualitatively different optima (noise-dominated flat fit vs near-interpolating fit) with similar LML. Bounds are necessary but not sufficient; log the chosen hyperparameters per round and treat abrupt jumps as a red flag. scikit-learn has no native hyperprior support — MAP requires a custom optimizer callable.

Closed-form LOO reuses hyperparameters fit on all n points, so it is mildly optimistic and does not account for hyperparameter-selection uncertainty; at n < ~30 spot-check with true refit-per-fold LOO.

Coverage/calibration statistics on 10-40 points have large binomial error (95% coverage estimated from 20 points is +/- ~10 points); use them as multi-round trends, not per-round gates, and be conservative about triggering recalibration.

Constant liar / Kriging believer results depend on the lie value and require frozen hyperparameters during fantasy refits; KB can chase phantom optima where the posterior mean extrapolates badly. Local penalization is sensitive to the Lipschitz-constant estimate.

Joint MC-qEI over all q*d coordinates simultaneously is unreliable without autodiff gradients; the greedy one-point-at-a-time construction (near-optimal by submodularity) is the practical numpy/scipy route.

The delta method breaks down when stage-1 uncertainty spans the steep region of a sigmoidal stage-2 response (exactly the light-off regime); default to MC propagation and use delta only as a cross-check.

RFF-based Thompson sampling degrades if too few features are used (m >= ~500 recommended) and is known to over-explore relative to EI-family acquisitions in low dimensions; the Matern spectral density is multivariate-t, not Gaussian — sampling it wrong (e.g. using the RBF Gaussian) silently changes the effective kernel.

Independent per-output GPs for the multi-output intermediate stage ignore cross-correlations between kinetic parameters; this typically widens (not narrows) propagated uncertainty but can misrank candidates when parameters are strongly correlated — noted as a v2 upgrade path (linked GPs / multi-task kernels).
Wasserstein/information-geometric simplex BO (Candelieri et al.) shows benefits mainly at high simplex dimension; at d <= 6 the added complexity is not justified by reported results.

The Digital Discovery 2025 batch-acquisition comparison used specific synthetic landscapes (Ackley, Hartmann) and one photovoltaics dataset; its ranking (MC acquisitions more noise-robust than serial UCB+LP) is a reasonable prior but should be re-verified on this campaign's own data via retrospective replay once a few rounds exist.

kinetics.summary:
CO2 methanation (Sabatier: CO2 + 4 H2 ⇌ CH4 + 2 H2O, ΔH°298 ≈ −165 kJ/mol) light-off/TPR data are fit at three levels of physical detail. (1) Empirical sigmoids (Boltzmann/logistic, Gompertz) are the most robust way to extract a light-off temperature T50 (and T90, max slope) from a single conversion-vs-T curve with no reactor assumptions; they cannot represent the high-T fall-off of the exothermic reversible reaction. (2) Lumped first-order plug-flow (integral) models give a physically meaningful, transferable rate: assuming an isothermal PFR slice at constant GHSV, an irreversible first-order reaction gives X(T)=1−exp(−k(T)·τ) with Arrhenius k(T); the reversible, equilibrium-capped generalization X(T)=Xeq(T)[1−exp(−k(T)·τ/Xeq(T))] reproduces the observed volcano-shaped CH4 curve (kinetic rise then thermodynamic decline). (3) Mechanistic LHHW rate laws — above all the Koschany, Schlereth & Hinrichsen (Appl. Catal. B 2016, 181, 504–516) expression for co-precipitated Ni/Al(O)x — capture product (water) inhibition and the slow approach to equilibrium across pressure/composition; this is the community-standard rate law and is widely reused verbatim in reactor and CFD models.

The Koschany rate is r = k·pH2^0.5·pCO2^0.5·(1 − pCH4·pH2O^2/(pCO2·pH2^4·Keq)) / (1 + K_OH·pH2O·pH2^−0.5 + K_H2·pH2^0.5 + K_mix·pCO2^0.5)^2, with the numerator carrying the driving-force term (1−Q/Keq) where Q=pCH4·pH2O^2/(pCO2·pH2^4) is the reaction quotient and Keq(T) is the (fixed, not fitted) thermodynamic constant, taken from the Lunde–Kester correlation. Reported best-fit values (reparameterized at Tref=555 K): k(Tref)≈3.46×10^−4 mol s^−1 g^−1 bar^−1, Ea≈77.5 kJ/mol; adsorption constants K_OH≈0.50 bar^−0.5, K_H2≈0.44 bar^−0.5, K_mix≈0.88 bar^−0.5 with van't Hoff enthalpies of order ±(6–25) kJ/mol. Across Ni/Al2O3, Ni/CeO2 and Ru catalysts, apparent activation energies cluster in 75–118 kJ/mol (Koschany 77.5, low-loaded Ni/Al2O3 ~80, Ni/CeO2 ~104), and power-law H2/CO2 orders run ~0.2–0.5 / ~0.1–0.3 with strong H2O inhibition.

The Eyring/TST form k=κ·(kB·T/h)·exp(ΔS‡/R)·exp(−ΔH‡/RT)=κ·(kB·T/h)·exp(−ΔG‡/RT) is chemically equivalent to Arrhenius over a normal 200–500 °C window (the extra linear-in-T prefactor is a small correction) but is preferred when you want thermodynamic activation parameters (ΔH‡, ΔS‡, ΔG‡), when comparing entropic effects across a catalyst library, or when tying fits to DFT-computed barriers; the mapping is Ea=ΔH‡+RT (surface/unimolecular) and A=(e·kB·T/h)·exp(ΔS‡/R).

For parameter estimation the dominant practical issue is the near-perfect correlation between ln(pre-exponential) and Ea; the fix is to fit the reparameterized Arrhenius k(T)=k_ref·exp[−(Ea/R)(1/T−1/Tref)] (and the analogous van't Hoff for each Ki), choosing Tref near the data centroid (in 1/T) to drive the k_ref–Ea correlation toward zero. Fit by weighted least squares (weights 1/σ_i^2 or relative 1/ŷ_i^2 for data spanning orders of magnitude), enforce positivity/exothermicity via log-parameters and bounds, and obtain uncertainties from the linearized covariance Cov(θ)=s^2·(JᵀWJ)^−1 (s^2=SSR/(N−p)), 95% CI = θ±t_{N−p,0.975}·√diag, with profile-likelihood or Monte-Carlo intervals when the confidence region is non-elliptic — exactly the uncertainty you then propagate into each figure of merit and hand to the GP as heteroscedastic noise.
key_equations_or_algorithms: STOICHIOMETRY & DRIVING FORCE. Sabatier reaction CO2 + 4 H2 ⇌ CH4 + 2 H2O, ΔH°(298K) ≈ −165 kJ/mol, Δn = −2 (so Keq has units bar^−2). Reaction quotient Q = (pCH4·pH2O^2)/(pCO2·pH2^4). Approach-to-equilibrium (dimensionless): β = Q/Keq ∈ [0,1]; driving-force factor η = (1 − Q/Keq) = 1 − β. Every rate law multiplies its kinetic part by η so that r→0 as the gas approaches equilibrium (β→1). p_i = partial pressures [bar], Keq = Keq(T) thermodynamic equilibrium constant.

EQUILIBRIUM CONSTANT (Lunde–Kester correlation, held FIXED not fitted). Keq(T) = exp[ (1/1.987)·(56000/T^2 + 34633/T − 16.4·ln T + 0.00557·T) + 33.165 ], T in K, Keq in atm^−2 (≈bar^−2). Alternatively compute Keq from Gibbs free energies: Keq(T) = exp(−ΔG_rxn°(T)/(R·T)) using NASA/Shomate polynomials or a Gibbs-minimizer. Use this Keq inside η above; do NOT fit it, to enforce thermodynamic consistency.

ARRHENIUS (standard). k(T) = A·exp(−Ea/(R·T)); A = pre-exponential [same units as k], Ea = activation energy [J/mol], R = 8.314 J/mol/K, T [K]. Linearized: ln k = ln A − (Ea/R)(1/T). Problem: cov(ln A, Ea) ≈ +1 (ill-conditioned).

ARRHENIUS REPARAMETERIZED (decorrelated — USE THIS). k(T) = k_ref·exp[ −(Ea/R)·(1/T − 1/Tref) ], where k_ref = k(Tref) is the rate constant AT the reference temperature. Choosing Tref near the harmonic/centroid temperature of the dataset, ideally Tref ≈ 1/⟨1/T⟩ over the fitted points, drives corr(k_ref, Ea) → 0, giving elliptical confidence regions and stable optimization (Schwaab & Pinto 2007). ln k_ref and Ea are then the fit parameters.

VAN'T HOFF for adsorption/inhibition constants (reparameterized identically). K_i(T) = K_i(Tref)·exp[ −(ΔH_i/R)·(1/T − 1/Tref) ]; ΔH_i = adsorption enthalpy [J/mol] (constrain exothermic ΔH_i<0 for true adsorption; some lumped constants in LHHW may be endothermic). K_i(Tref) fitted as a log-parameter to enforce positivity.

EYRING / TRANSITION-STATE THEORY. k = κ·(kB·T/h)·exp(−ΔG‡/(R·T)) = κ·(kB·T/h)·exp(ΔS‡/R)·exp(−ΔH‡/(R·T)). kB = 1.381e-23 J/K, h = 6.626e-34 J·s, κ = transmission coefficient (≈1), ΔG‡/ΔH‡/ΔS‡ = Gibbs/enthalpy/entropy of activation. Linearized (Eyring plot): ln(k/T) = −(ΔH‡/R)·(1/T) + [ ln(kB/h) + ΔS‡/R ]; slope→ΔH‡, intercept→ΔS‡. Arrhenius↔Eyring mapping: Ea = ΔH‡ + R·T (unimolecular/surface step) or ΔH‡ + 2RT (gas bimolecular); A = (e·kB·T/h)·exp(ΔS‡/R). Prefer Eyring when reporting ΔH‡/ΔS‡/ΔG‡, comparing entropic effects across a catalyst library, or linking to DFT barriers; Arrhenius is adequate over a narrow TPR window.

KOSCHANY 2016 LHHW RATE LAW (Ni/Al(O)x, community standard). r = k·pH2^0.5·pCO2^0.5·(1 − pCH4·pH2O^2/(pCO2·pH2^4·Keq)) / (1 + K_OH·pH2O·pH2^(−0.5) + K_H2·pH2^0.5 + K_mix·pCO2^0.5)^2. r in mol s^−1 g_cat^−1; numerator = kinetic term × driving force η; denominator (squared) = surface-coverage/inhibition term. K_OH·pH2O·pH2^−0.5 term encodes water (hydroxyl) inhibition — the dominant product-inhibition effect. Best-fit parameters (reparameterized, Tref = 555 K): k(Tref) ≈ 3.46×10^−4 mol s^−1 g^−1 bar^−1, Ea ≈ 77.5 kJ/mol; K_OH(Tref) ≈ 0.50 bar^−0.5 (ΔH_OH ≈ +22.4 kJ/mol); K_H2(Tref) ≈ 0.44 bar^−0.5 (ΔH_H2 ≈ −6.2 kJ/mol); K_mix(Tref) ≈ 0.88 bar^−0.5 (ΔH_mix ≈ −10 kJ/mol). (Verify the three adsorption enthalpies against Table in the paper; the functional form and k/Ea are well established.)

POWER-LAW RATE WITH INHIBITION & EQUILIBRIUM (simple, few parameters). r = k(T)·pH2^m·pCO2^n·(1 − Q/Keq) / (1 + K_H2O·pH2O/pH2^0.5)^2 (inhibition optional). Typical fitted magnitudes for Ni: apparent Ea ≈ 75–118 kJ/mol (Koschany 77.5, low-loaded Ni/Al2O3 ~80, Ni/CeO2 ~104); H2 order m ≈ 0.2–0.5, CO2 order n ≈ 0.1–0.3; water adsorption/inhibition constant O(1–3) atm^−1. Reduces to pseudo-first-order in the limiting reactant when one partial pressure dominates.

INTEGRAL PLUG-FLOW LIGHT-OFF (irreversible first order). Isothermal PFR slice, constant GHSV: X(T) = 1 − exp(−k(T)·τ) = 1 − exp(−Da), Damköhler Da = k(T)·τ. τ = residence time = V_cat/Q_vol = 1/GHSV [s]; for a weight-based intrinsic rate use Da = k(T)·W_cat/F_CO2,0 (k then in appropriate mol/kg/s/bar units). k(T) Arrhenius (reparameterized). This is the canonical light-off fit for conversion-vs-T at fixed feed.

REVERSIBLE, EQUILIBRIUM-CAPPED FIRST ORDER (reproduces volcano CH4 curve). X(T) = Xeq(T)·[ 1 − exp( −k(T)·τ / Xeq(T) ) ]. Limits: kτ→0 ⇒ X→k·τ (kinetic rise); kτ→∞ ⇒ X→Xeq(T) (thermodynamic ceiling). Xeq(T) computed from Keq(T) at the feed stoichiometry (root-find on Q(X)=Keq). Captures the high-T decline of CH4 yield that pure sigmoids cannot.

BOLTZMANN / LOGISTIC SIGMOID (robust T50 extraction, model-free). X(T) = X_max / (1 + exp(−(T − T50)/dT)). T50 = inflection = temperature at 50% of X_max [K]; dT = slope width [K] (smaller dT = sharper light-off). Max slope at T50: (dX/dT)|T50 = X_max/(4·dT). Order-of-magnitude link to apparent activation energy near T50: Ea,app ≈ R·T50^2/dT (steeper curve ⇒ larger Ea). Fit X_max, T50, dT by nonlinear least squares.

GOMPERTZ SIGMOID (asymmetric alternative). X(T) = X_max·exp(−exp(−(T − b)/c)). b = location [K] (inflection / max-slope point, where X = X_max/e ≈ 0.368·X_max); c = scale [K]. T50 (half of X_max) solves exp(−exp(−(T50−b)/c)) = 0.5 ⇒ T50 = b + c·(−ln(ln 2)) = b + 0.3665·c. Use when the light-off rise is visibly asymmetric.

FIGURE-OF-MERIT: INTEGRAL CH4 (baseline objective). FOM = ∫_{T_low}^{T_high} y_CH4(T) dT (or ∫ X_CH4 dT), evaluated by trapezoid/Simpson on the fitted curve; normalize by (T_high−T_low) for a mean-yield FOM. Rewards both early light-off and a high plateau. Complementary scalar FOMs: T50, T90, max CH4 yield y_max and its T_opt, integral CH4 formation rate, and Ea,app. All are deterministic functionals g(θ) of the fitted curve parameters θ.

PARAMETER ESTIMATION: WEIGHTED LEAST SQUARES + COVARIANCE. Objective: minimize S(θ) = Σ_i w_i·(y_i − ŷ_i(θ))^2, weights w_i = 1/σ_i^2 (known measurement variance) or w_i = 1/ŷ_i^2 (relative error, for responses spanning orders of magnitude). Solve with Levenberg–Marquardt from a multistart / global (differential-evolution) seed. Linearized parameter covariance: Cov(θ) = s^2·(JᵀWJ)^−1, with Jacobian J_ij = ∂ŷ_i/∂θ_j at the optimum, W = diag(w_i), residual variance s^2 = S(θ*)/(N−p). Standard errors SE_j = √(Cov_jj); 95% CI: θ_j ± t_{N−p,0.975}·SE_j; parameter correlation matrix ρ_jk = Cov_jk/(SE_j·SE_k) — inspect to confirm reparameterization killed the k_ref–Ea correlation. Use profile-likelihood or Bayesian/MCMC intervals when the confidence region is non-elliptic.

UNCERTAINTY PROPAGATION FROM CURVE FIT INTO FOM (feeds the GP). For any scalar FOM g(θ): delta method σ_FOM^2 = (∂g/∂θ)ᵀ·Cov(θ)·(∂g/∂θ). For the integral FOM, ∂g/∂θ_j = ∫ (∂ŷ(T;θ)/∂θ_j) dT (integrate the parameter-sensitivities). More robust for nonlinear g: Monte-Carlo — sample θ^(s) ~ N(θ*, Cov(θ)) (or from MCMC posterior), compute g(θ^(s)) for s=1..S, take mean and variance. The resulting (FOM, σ_FOM^2) per experiment is the observation and heteroscedastic noise variance passed to the GP (e.g. GaussianProcessRegressor alpha = σ_FOM^2 per point).
design_recommendations: Fit each light-off/TPR curve with a small MODEL CASCADE and keep them all: (a) Boltzmann logistic for a fast, assumption-free T50/T90/dT; (b) reversible equilibrium-capped first-order X(T)=Xeq(T)[1−exp(−k τ/Xeq)] for a transferable Arrhenius k(T), Ea and to reproduce the high-T CH4 fall-off; (c) OPTIONAL Koschany LHHW only when you have data across multiple pressures/feed compositions (needs partial-pressure profiles, not just X vs T). For single-feed TPR, (a)+(b) are sufficient and far better conditioned.

ALWAYS fit the reparameterized Arrhenius k(T)=k_ref·exp[−(Ea/R)(1/T−1/Tref)] and reparameterized van't Hoff for any Ki, with Tref set programmatically to the per-curve data centroid Tref=1/mean(1/T_data). This is a one-line change that removes the k_ref–Ea correlation and stabilizes every downstream covariance. Expose Tref in the fitted-model metadata.

Use lmfit (or scipy.optimize.least_squares + manual covariance) rather than bare curve_fit: it gives named/bounded parameters, log-transform for positivity (k_ref, Ki>0), weighted residuals, .covar for Cov(θ), and .conf_interval() for profile-likelihood CIs when the region is non-elliptic. Store the full Cov(θ), not just SEs — you need the off-diagonals for FOM propagation.

Treat Keq(T) as a FIXED input (Lunde–Kester correlation or a Gibbs-minimization helper), never a fit parameter, and build the (1−Q/Keq) driving-force factor from it. Provide Xeq(T) via a small equilibrium solver (root-find Q(X)=Keq at the feed) so the reversible model and any LHHW share one thermodynamics module. This enforces consistency and lets the fit approach equilibrium correctly at high T.

Define figures of merit as pure functionals g(θ) of the fitted curve so uncertainty propagation is mechanical: baseline FOM = ∫ y_CH4(T) dT (trapz on a dense T-grid of the fitted curve), plus T50, T90, y_max, T_opt, Ea_app. Compute each FOM's variance by BOTH the delta method (σ^2=∇g·Cov·∇gᵀ, ∇g by autodiff or finite differences) and a Monte-Carlo cross-check (sample θ~N(θ*,Cov), recompute g); ship σ_FOM to the GP as per-point noise.

Weight the curve fits: if replicate/instrument noise on outlet concentrations is known, use w_i=1/σ_i^2; otherwise use relative weighting w_i=1/ŷ_i^2 because CH4/CO/CO2 span orders of magnitude across the light-off. Fit CH4, CO and CO2 jointly with a mass-balance/closure constraint (Σ carbon conserved) to reduce degeneracy and get a consistent selectivity.

Make the fitter robust: multistart or differential_evolution global seed → Levenberg–Marquardt refine; bound Ea∈[40,160] kJ/mol, orders∈[0,1], adsorption ΔH exothermic where physical; flag and quarantine curves where the covariance is ill-conditioned (large condition number of JᵀWJ) or CIs blow up, so the active-learner is not fed garbage-uncertainty points.

Persist a structured record per experiment: {selected_composition, measured_composition, raw curve, chosen model + Tref, θ*, Cov(θ), all FOMs with σ, fit diagnostics (R^2, reduced χ^2, condition number)}. The GP chain then maps composition→θ or composition→FOM with input-noise on composition (measured≠selected) AND output-noise σ_FOM — both must flow through so batch Bayesian optimization sees honest uncertainty.

For the batch-BO layer, remember Ea and k_ref (or T50) are smoother, more Gaussian-behaved responses over the metal-fraction simplex than the raw integral FOM; consider modeling k_ref/Ea (or log-FOM) with the GP and deriving the integral-CH4 FOM analytically, which stabilizes the surrogate and keeps uncertainty interpretable.

Keep the LHHW/Koschany parameters (k=3.46e-4 mol/s/g/bar @555K, Ea=77.5 kJ/mol, K_OH/K_H2/K_mix) as a documented default in a physical-priors module: even when not fitting LHHW, they seed sensible Ea priors (~75–118 kJ/mol for Ni), bound the sigmoid Ea_app, and provide a physics baseline curve to sanity-check fits and detect outlier experiments.

caveats: Direct page fetches (WebFetch and curl) were blocked by this environment's egress policy for ScienceDirect, Wiley, ACS, MDPI, PMC, Wikipedia and repository PDFs; findings were assembled from WebSearch result summaries across multiple independent sources plus established domain knowledge. The Koschany LHHW FUNCTIONAL FORM and k/Ea (77.5 kJ/mol, Tref=555 K) are high-confidence and cross-corroborated; the three adsorption-constant enthalpies (ΔH_OH≈+22.4, ΔH_H2≈−6.2, ΔH_mix≈−10 kJ/mol) and K_i(Tref) values should be verified against Table 5 of the original 2016 paper before hard-coding.

The Lunde–Kester Keq(T) coefficient placement varies slightly between transcriptions (the additive 33.165 vs whether it sits inside or outside the 1/1.987 factor); validate the implementation against a Gibbs-energy calculation (Keq from ΔG_rxn°(T)) at a few temperatures (e.g. 250–400 °C) before use. Keq units are pressure^−2 (bar^−2 or atm^−2) because Δn=−2.

The Ea,app ≈ R·T50^2/dT link between logistic-sigmoid slope and apparent activation energy is an order-of-magnitude relation, not exact; it depends on the underlying rate order and on external mass-transfer limitations, which flatten the light-off slope and bias Ea_app low. Check for transport limitations (Weisz–Prater, Mears) before interpreting sigmoid slopes as intrinsic kinetics.

The equilibrium-capped reversible first-order closed form X(T)=Xeq[1−exp(−kτ/Xeq)] is an engineering approximation (exact only for a genuinely first-order reversible reaction in an isothermal PFR); real TPR runs have axial temperature gradients and non-first-order kinetics, so treat its k(T)/Ea as effective/apparent, not intrinsic.

Because selected composition ≠ measured composition, there is input noise on the GP features; propagate it (e.g. GP with input uncertainty, or model on measured composition with a composition-error term) in addition to the σ_FOM output noise derived here — both are needed for honest batch Bayesian optimization.

Power-law reaction orders and Ea vary with catalyst, loading, and conditions (differential vs equilibrium-limited); the quoted ranges (H2 order 0.2–0.5, CO2 0.1–0.3, Ea 75–118 kJ/mol) are Ni-centric — Ru and multimetallic/zeolite-supported systems can differ, so use them as priors, not fixed values.
